101463.q: Which big bird of prey builds its nest high up in rainforest giants?
101463.e: The harpy eagle is a mighty bird of prey from the rainforest. It builds its nest in the crowns of very tall trees.
101463.m: The harpy eagle nests in rainforest giants.

101464.q: On which continent does the Amazon flow?
101464.e: The Amazon flows through South America, mainly through Peru and Brazil.
101464.m: The Amazon flows in South America.

101465.e: The Amazon is a huge river. The largest rainforest on Earth grows around it.
101465.m: The Amazon is a big river.

101466.q: In which country is most of the Amazon rainforest?
101466.e: About 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil.
101466.m: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil.

101467.q: Into which ocean does the Amazon flow?
101467.e: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic Ocean on the coast of Brazil.
101467.m: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic.

101468.q: What colour are many river dolphins in the Amazon?
101468.e: The Amazon river dolphin often turns pink with age. That is why it is also called the pink river dolphin.
101468.m: Pink dolphins live in the Amazon.

101469.q: Which plant on the Amazon has round leaves that grow more than two metres wide?
101469.e: The giant water lily grows in the Amazon region. Its floating leaves can grow up to about three metres wide.
101469.m: The giant water lily has huge round leaves.

101470.q: Which river in the world carries the most water?
101470.e: No other river carries as much water into the sea as the Amazon.
101470.m: The Amazon is the river with the most water in the world.

101471.q: What is almost completely missing in a desert?
101471.e: In a desert it rains very rarely. That is why only a few plants grow there.
101471.m: It rains very little in the desert.

101472.q: Which desert animal has a hump on its back?
101472.e: The dromedary has one hump. It stores fat in it as a reserve.

101473.q: What happens in many deserts at night?
101473.e: In the daytime it is hot, but at night the desert cools down a lot. There are no clouds to hold the warmth in.
101473.m: It can get cold in the desert at night.

101474.q: What is a hill of sand shaped by the wind called?
101474.e: The wind blows sand together into hills. These hills of sand are called dunes.
101474.m: A dune is a hill of sand.

101475.q: Which area also counts as a desert because it has very little precipitation?
101475.e: A desert does not have to be hot. So little precipitation falls in Antarctica that it counts as a cold desert.

101476.q: Which animal with a venomous sting on its tail lives in deserts?
101476.e: Scorpions often live in deserts. There is a venomous sting at the end of their tail.
101476.m: The scorpion has a sting on its tail.

101477.q: Where does the water in an oasis usually come from?
101477.e: There is often groundwater under the desert. In the oasis it comes out as a spring or is drawn from wells.
101477.m: Oases usually get their water from the ground.

101478.q: Why do caravans stop at oases?
101478.e: There is hardly any water in the desert. The people and animals of a caravan drink at the oasis and fill up their supplies.
101478.m: Travellers get water at the oasis.

101479.q: What is a group of travellers with camels in the desert called?
101479.e: A caravan travels through the desert with camels and goods, often from oasis to oasis.
101479.m: A caravan travels through the desert with camels.

101480.q: What is a mirage in the desert?
a: A picture that is not real
101480.e: In great heat the air reflects things. Some travellers then think they see water in the distance, but it is not there at all.
101480.m: A mirage is an optical illusion.

101481.q: How much water can a thirsty dromedary drink at an oasis in one go?
101481.e: A dromedary can go a very long time without water. When it finds water, it drinks a great deal in a few minutes, up to about 100 litres.
101481.m: A thirsty dromedary can drink a lot of water in one go.

101482.q: In which country is the famous Siwa Oasis?
101482.e: Siwa lies in the desert in the west of Egypt, near the border with Libya.
101482.m: The Siwa Oasis is in Egypt.

101483.q: What do the palms in the oasis give people?
101483.e: The palms protect against the hot sun. Other plants also grow better under them.
101483.m: Palms give shade in the oasis.

101484.q: What do people use the long leaves of the date palm for?
101484.e: People weave baskets and mats from the leaves of the date palm. They also use them to cover roofs.
101484.m: You can weave baskets from palm leaves.

101485.q: Where do date palms like to grow?
101485.e: Date palms love heat. But they need water in the ground, for example in an oasis.
101485.m: Date palms grow in hot areas.

101486.q: How do dates hang on the palm?
101486.e: Dates grow in big, heavy bunches at the top under the leaves.
101486.m: Dates hang in bunches on the palm.

101487.q: What is often done with dates so that they keep for a long time?
101487.e: Dried dates keep for a long time. That is how we know them from the shops in Switzerland too.
101487.m: Dried dates keep for a long time.

101488.e: Inside every date there is a hard, long stone. A new palm can grow from it.
101488.m: There is a hard stone inside a date.

101489.q: What do succulents store in their thick leaves or stems?
101489.e: Succulents are plants that store water. That way they survive long dry periods.

101490.q: Which of these plants is a succulent?
101490.e: The cactus stores water in its thick stem. That is why it is a succulent.

101491.q: What do many cacti have instead of green leaves?
101491.e: In many cacti the leaves have turned into spines. The spines protect against animals and lose hardly any water.
101491.m: Cacti have spines instead of leaves.

101492.q: Where do wild cacti like to grow best?
a: Where it is hot and dry
101492.e: Cacti store water in their thick stem. That is why they can live in hot, dry areas such as deserts.
101492.m: Cacti live where it is hot and dry.

101493.q: Which succulent is often found in skin creams?
101493.e: Aloe vera has thick leaves full of gel. This gel is often used in creams.
101493.m: Aloe vera has leaves full of gel.

101494.q: Which succulent also grows on rocks in the Swiss Alps?
101494.e: The houseleek has thick leaves in rosettes. It grows on dry, sunny rocks, in the Alps too.
101494.m: The houseleek grows on rocks in the Alps.

101495.q: On which continent do most cacti grow wild?
101495.e: Almost all cacti come from America, for example from Mexico and the USA. People later planted them on other continents.

101496.q: How often do you need to water a succulent indoors?
101496.e: Succulents need little water. Too much water makes their roots rot.

101497.q: Why do hardly any trees grow in the tundra?
101497.e: In the tundra it is very cold for a long time, and the summer is short. Trees cannot grow there.
101497.m: The tundra is too cold for trees.

101498.q: Which animals roam the tundra in big herds?
101498.e: Reindeer move through the tundra in big herds. In North America they are called caribou.

101499.q: What mainly grows in the tundra?
101499.e: Low plants such as mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs grow in the tundra.
101499.m: Mosses and lichens grow in the tundra.

101500.q: Which animal with a white winter coat lives in the tundra?
101500.e: The Arctic fox has a white coat in winter. That way it is well camouflaged in the snow.
101500.m: The Arctic fox is white in winter.

101501.q: What happens in summer in the far north?
101501.e: In summer the sun does not set for days in the far north. This is called the midnight sun.
101501.m: In summer the midnight sun shines in the far north.

101502.q: Which small animal with a bushy tail gets seeds out of cones in the taiga?
101502.e: The squirrel lives in coniferous forests such as the taiga. It gnaws cones open and eats the seeds inside.
101502.m: The squirrel likes eating seeds from cones.

101503.q: Which big animal with broad, flat antlers lives in the taiga?
101503.e: The elk, called moose in North America, is the biggest deer in the world. The males have broad, flat antlers.
101503.m: The elk lives in the taiga.

101504.q: In which country is a huge part of the taiga?
101504.e: In Siberia in Russia, the taiga stretches for thousands of kilometres.
101504.m: A large part of the taiga is in Russia.

101505.q: Which bear lives in the forests of the taiga?
101505.e: The brown bear lives in the forests of the taiga. In winter it rests in a cave.
101505.m: The brown bear lives in the taiga.

101506.q: Which big wild cat lives in the taiga in eastern Russia?
101506.e: The Siberian tiger, also called the Amur tiger, lives in the forests of eastern Russia.
101506.m: The Siberian tiger lives in the taiga.

101507.q: Which water can mangroves cope with?
101507.e: Most plants die in salt water. Mangroves can live with it.

101508.e: At high tide the sea rises and floods the mangroves. At low tide the ground dries out again.
101508.m: At high tide mangroves stand in the sea.

101509.q: Which monkey with a very big nose lives in mangroves on Borneo?
101509.e: The proboscis monkey lives on the island of Borneo in mangroves and forests along rivers. It can swim well.
101509.m: The proboscis monkey lives in the mangroves of Borneo.

101510.q: Which crab waves a big claw in the mangroves?
101510.e: In fiddler crabs, the male has one very big claw. It waves with it.
101510.m: The fiddler crab waves its big claw.

101511.q: What mainly grows in the savannah?
101511.e: A savannah is a wide grassland with scattered trees and bushes.
101511.m: A lot of grass grows in the savannah.

101512.q: Which animal with a long neck eats leaves from tall trees in the savannah?
101512.e: With its long neck the giraffe reaches leaves high up in the trees.
101512.m: The giraffe has a long neck.

101513.q: Which tree with a very thick trunk grows in the African savannah?
101513.e: The baobab, also called the monkey bread tree, stores water in its thick trunk.
101513.m: The baobab has a very thick trunk.

101514.q: Which striped animals live in herds in the savannah?
101514.e: Zebras have black and white stripes and live in herds in the African savannah.
101514.m: Zebras live in herds in the savannah.

101515.q: Which wild cat is the fastest land animal and lives in the savannah?
101515.e: For a short time the cheetah can run at over 90 kilometres per hour.
101515.m: The cheetah is the fastest land animal.

101516.q: Which two seasons are there in the savannah?
101516.e: In the savannah a rainy season and a dry season take turns.
101516.m: In the savannah there is a rainy season and a dry season.

101517.q: Which tree with a flat, umbrella-shaped crown is typical of the savannah?
101517.e: The umbrella thorn acacia has a wide, flat crown like an umbrella. Giraffes like eating its leaves.
101517.m: The umbrella thorn acacia looks like an umbrella.

101518.q: Which big bird that cannot fly lives in the African savannah?
101518.e: The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it can run very fast. The emu lives in Australia.
101518.m: The ostrich is the biggest bird.

101519.q: Which largest land animal lives in the African savannah?
101519.e: The African elephant is the biggest animal that lives on land.
101519.m: The elephant is the biggest land animal.

101608.q: Which parts of the body does a sun hat with a wide brim protect?
101608.e: The wide brim casts shade on the face, ears and neck. The hat itself covers the head.
101608.m: A hat with a wide brim protects your head, face and neck.

101609.q: What is the rim of a hat called?
101609.e: The rim that sticks out from a hat is called the brim. The wider the brim, the more shade it gives.
101609.m: The rim of a hat is called the brim.

101610.q: Which colour of hat gets less hot in the sun?
101610.e: Light colours reflect a lot of sunlight. Dark colours absorb the light and get hot.
101610.m: Light clothes and hats stay cooler in the sun.

101611.q: What does a cap with neck protection have at the back?
a: A piece of fabric over the neck
101611.e: With this cap, a piece of fabric hangs down at the back. It protects the neck from sunburn.
101611.m: Neck protection covers the neck with fabric.

101612.q: Why should small children wear a hat in the sun?
a: Their head is sensitive to the sun
101612.e: Children's scalps are often not well covered by hair, and their skin is sensitive. A hat protects against sunburn and overheating.
101612.m: Children always wear a hat in the sun.

a: A hat made of woven straw
101613.e: Straw hats are woven from dried stalks. They are light and let air through.
101613.m: A straw hat is light and airy.

101614.q: When is a sun hat most important?
a: At midday when it is very sunny
Early in the morning in bed
101614.e: At midday, the sun is highest and strongest. That is when your head needs the most protection.
101614.m: At midday, your head needs the most sun protection.

101615.q: What is the strap under the chin on some sun hats for?
a: So the wind does not blow the hat away
101615.e: The chin strap holds the hat firmly on your head. That way it stays on even in the wind or while you play.
101615.m: A chin strap holds your hat on in the wind.

101616.q: Can we see UV rays with our eyes?
101616.e: UV rays are a part of sunlight that our eyes cannot see. Even so, they affect our skin and eyes.
101616.m: UV rays are invisible, but they still have an effect.

101617.q: Where does most of the UV radiation that reaches us come from?
101617.e: As well as light and warmth, the sun also sends out UV rays. It is our biggest source of UV.
101617.m: Most UV radiation comes from the sun.

101618.q: What can too much UV radiation do to your skin?
a: Cause a gap in your teeth
101618.e: UV rays damage the skin. It turns red, gets hot and hurts.
101618.m: Too much UV radiation causes sunburn.

101619.q: Does UV radiation also get through clouds?
101619.e: Clouds only block part of the UV radiation. That is why you can get sunburnt on cloudy days too.
101619.m: Even when it is cloudy, the sun can burn your skin.

a: In the shade of a house
101620.e: In the mountains, the layer of air above us is thinner. It blocks less UV radiation.
101620.m: The sun is stronger in the mountains than in the valley.

101621.q: Which layer high up in the air blocks a lot of UV radiation?
101621.e: The ozone layer lies high above the Earth. It absorbs a large part of the dangerous UV radiation.
101621.m: The ozone layer protects us from a lot of UV radiation.

101622.q: Why does your skin go brown in summer?
a: It is protecting itself from UV rays
101622.e: In the sun, the skin makes more dark pigment. This protects a little against UV rays, but not enough.
101622.m: Tanned skin is a sign that your skin is defending itself.

101623.q: Apart from the skin, which parts of the body can UV rays also damage?
101623.e: UV rays can irritate the eyes and damage them over time. Good sunglasses help.
101623.m: Your eyes also need protection from UV rays.

a: A lot of sun on your head and neck
101624.e: If the sun shines for a long time on an unprotected head and neck, the brain gets irritated. This is called sunstroke.
101624.m: Sunstroke comes from too much sun on your head.

101625.q: What is a typical sign of sunstroke?
101625.e: With sunstroke, your head often hurts. You may also feel dizzy and sick and have a red, hot head.
101625.m: A headache after a lot of sun can be sunstroke.

101626.q: What do you do first if someone has sunstroke?
a: Carry on playing in the sun
101626.e: The person must get out of the sun at once. In the shade, the head can recover.
101626.m: With sunstroke, go into the shade at once.

101627.q: What do you cool the head with if someone has sunstroke?
101627.e: Cool, wet cloths on the head and neck help. They take away heat.
101627.m: Cool cloths help a hot head.

101628.q: How does the head often feel with sunstroke?
101628.e: With sunstroke, the head is usually hot and red. The rest of the body, however, can be normally warm.
101628.m: A hot, red head fits with sunstroke.

101629.e: A hat or cap keeps the sun off your head. That way the brain does not overheat.
101629.m: A hat is the best protection against sunstroke.

101630.q: How should a person with sunstroke lie?
a: On their tummy in the sun
101630.e: You raise the upper body and head a little. That takes pressure off the head.
101630.m: With sunstroke, the head lies a little higher.

101631.q: What should someone with sunstroke drink?
101631.e: If the person is conscious, they may drink water in sips. That replaces the fluid they have lost.
101631.m: After a lot of sun, drink water in small sips.

a: The whole body gets too hot
101632.e: With heatstroke, the body can no longer get rid of its heat. The body temperature rises dangerously high.
101632.m: Heatstroke means the whole body overheats.

101633.e: Heatstroke can be life-threatening. You must get help immediately.

101634.q: Where must you never leave children and animals alone in summer?
a: In the garden in the shade
At the swimming pool with supervision
101634.e: A car in the sun gets very hot inside very quickly. That can lead to heatstroke.
101634.m: In summer, nobody stays alone in a parked car.

101635.q: What helps against heatstroke on hot days?
101635.e: If you drink enough, you can sweat and cool your body that way. That helps prevent heatstroke.
101635.m: On hot days, drink lots of water.

101636.q: When should you not do tiring sport on hot days?
a: At midday and in the afternoon
101636.e: It is hottest at midday and in the afternoon. Sport is better early in the morning or in the evening.
101636.m: In summer, it is better to do sport in the morning or evening.

101637.q: How high can body temperature rise with heatstroke?
101637.e: Normal is about 37 degrees Celsius. With heatstroke, the temperature often rises above 40 degrees.
101637.m: A body temperature over 40 degrees is dangerous.

101638.q: How do you cool someone with heatstroke until help arrives?
101638.e: You take the person to a cool place and cool them with damp cloths. At the same time, you call the emergency number.
101638.m: When overheated, the body needs shade and cooling.

101639.e: An object blocks the light. Behind it, there is a darker area: the shadow.
101639.m: A shadow forms where something blocks the light.

101640.e: At midday, the sun is highest. The light falls steeply from above, and the shadow is short.
101640.m: Your shadow is shortest at midday.

101641.q: Your shadow is shorter than you. What does that mean?
a: The sun is strong, protect yourself
101641.e: If your shadow is shorter than you, the sun is high. Then UV radiation is strong.
101641.m: If your shadow is short, you need sun protection.

101642.q: Why is it cooler in the shade?
a: The sun does not shine directly there
101642.e: In the shade, the warm rays of the sun do not hit us directly. That is why it is more pleasant there.
101642.m: In the shade, the sun does not warm you directly.

101643.q: What is a large umbrella that gives shade called?
101643.e: A parasol keeps off the sun's rays. Underneath it is shady and cooler.

101644.q: Does shade protect you completely from UV rays?
101644.e: Some UV radiation reaches you even in the shade, for example from the sky and from bright surfaces. That is why you still need sun cream.
101644.m: Even in the shade, you need some sun protection.

a: In the morning and in the evening
101645.e: In the morning and evening, the sun is low. The light comes in at a flat angle and makes long shadows.
101645.m: A low sun makes long shadows.

101646.q: What does the abbreviation SPF on sun cream stand for?
101646.e: SPF stands for sun protection factor. It shows how strongly the cream protects against sunburn.
101646.m: The sun protection factor shows how strong the sun cream is.

101647.q: Which sun protection factor protects most strongly?
101647.e: The higher the number, the stronger the protection. SPF 50 protects more than SPF 30 or 15.
101647.m: The higher the sun protection factor, the stronger the protection.

101648.q: What must you do with sun cream after swimming?
a: Let it dry and leave it
101648.e: Water and drying yourself rub some of the cream off. That is why you put more on afterwards.
101648.m: After swimming, put on more sun cream.

101649.q: When is the best time to put on sun cream?
a: Before going out in the sun
Only once your skin is red
101649.e: The cream should already be working when the sun hits your skin. That is why you put it on before going out.
101649.m: Sun cream goes on before you go outside.

101650.q: Which places do people often forget when putting on sun cream?
a: The soles of the feet inside shoes
101650.e: Ears, neck and nose get lots of sun. But they are easy to forget when putting on cream.
101650.m: Your ears and neck need sun cream too.

101651.q: How much sun cream should you use?
101651.e: With too little cream, the sun protection factor does not work properly. You should apply it generously.
101651.m: Sun cream must be applied generously.

101652.q: Does sun cream protect you all day without a break?
a: No, you have to put more on
101652.e: Sweat, water and rubbing remove the cream. That is why you have to put more on during the day.
101652.m: You have to reapply sun cream during the day.

101653.q: What sun protection factor do children need at least?
a: A high one, about 30 or more
101653.e: Children's skin is sensitive and burns quickly. That is why a high sun protection factor is recommended.
101653.m: Children's skin needs a high sun protection factor.

101654.q: What does the UV index show?
a: How strong the UV radiation is
101654.e: The UV index is a number for the strength of UV radiation. The higher the number, the faster you get sunburnt.
101654.m: The UV index measures the strength of UV radiation.

101655.q: What does a high UV index mean?
101655.e: With a high UV index, skin gets sunburnt quickly. Then you need a hat, clothes and sun cream.
101655.m: A high UV index means lots of sun protection.

101656.q: From which UV index should you protect yourself?
101656.e: Sun protection is recommended from a UV index of 3. Below 3, the radiation is low.
101656.m: From UV index 3, you need sun protection.

101657.q: What is best at midday when the UV index is high?
a: Lying in the sun for a long time
101657.e: UV radiation is strongest at midday. When the UV index is high, you look for shade at this time.
101657.m: When the UV index is high, stay in the shade at midday.

101658.q: At what time of day is the UV index usually highest?
a: Late at 9 o'clock in the evening
101658.e: At midday, the sun is highest. Then UV radiation is strongest.
101658.m: The UV index is highest around midday.

101659.q: In which season is the UV index in the lowlands usually highest?
101659.e: In summer, the sun is very high at midday. That is why UV radiation is strongest then.
101659.m: UV radiation is strongest in summer.

101660.q: What does a UV index of 11 or more mean?
101660.e: Values of 11 and above count as extreme. Unprotected skin then burns very quickly.
101660.m: A UV index of 11 or more is extreme.

101661.q: Where can you find tomorrow's UV index?
101661.e: Many weather forecasts and weather apps show the UV index. That way you can be prepared.
101661.m: The weather forecast often shows the UV index too.

101662.q: How does a dog, which hardly sweats, cool down?
a: It pants with its mouth open
101662.e: Dogs only have a few sweat glands, mainly on their paws. They cool down mainly by panting.

101663.q: Which clothes feel comfortable when you sweat in summer?
a: Several jackets on top of each other
101663.e: Airy clothes let sweat evaporate. That way the body can cool itself better.
101663.m: In summer, wear light, airy clothes.

101664.e: Chilblains are red or bluish swellings of the skin. They often itch or burn.
101664.m: A chilblain is an itchy swelling caused by cold.

101665.e: Chilblains form mainly on fingers, toes and sometimes the ears. These places cool down quickly.
101665.m: Chilblains often appear on fingers and toes.

101666.q: Which weather makes chilblains more likely?
101666.e: Chilblains form in damp cold, even when it is not below zero. Wet socks are a typical cause.

101667.q: How does a chilblain often feel?
a: It is ice cold and hard as glass
101667.e: Chilblains often itch and burn, especially when you come back into the warm. That is unpleasant.

101668.q: What protects your feet from chilblains?
101668.e: Dry, warm socks keep your feet warm. Wet socks chill the skin.
101668.m: Dry, warm socks protect your feet.

101669.q: Are chilblains the same as frostbite?
a: No, the skin is not frozen
101669.e: With chilblains, the skin is not frozen but irritated by damp cold. With frostbite, on the other hand, tissue freezes.

101670.q: What do you do if you have been playing in the snow with wet gloves?
a: Carry on playing with wet ones
Put your hands in the snow
Put the gloves on the ice
101670.e: Wet gloves chill your hands quickly. Dry gloves keep them warm again.
101670.m: Swap wet gloves for dry ones.

101671.q: What colour is the skin often with a chilblain?
101671.e: Chilblains are usually red or bluish. The area is often swollen too.

101672.e: In great cold, tissue can freeze. That damages the skin and the parts underneath.

101673.q: Which parts of the body are most likely to get frostbite?
101673.e: Fingers, toes, nose and ears are far from the inside of the body. They cool down fastest.
101673.m: Fingers, toes, nose and ears get frostbite first.

101674.q: What does frostbitten skin often look like?
101674.e: Frostbitten skin is often white, grey or waxy. It feels hard and cold.
101674.m: Frostbitten skin is often white and hard.

101675.q: What do you often feel in a frostbitten spot?
101675.e: Because of the cold, the nerves work badly. The spot feels numb.

101676.q: Should you rub frostbitten skin with snow?
101676.e: Rubbing with snow injures the skin even more and cools it further. That is an old mistake.
101676.m: Never rub frostbitten skin with snow.

101677.q: What is the right way to warm a frostbitten spot?
a: Slowly, for example with body heat
101677.e: You warm it gently, for example in the armpit or with lukewarm water. Too much heat harms the skin.

101678.q: Why does cold feel stronger when it is windy?
a: The wind takes away more heat
The wind only dries your hair
101678.e: Wind blows away the warm air right next to the skin. That way the body cools down faster.

101679.q: What protects your fingers from frostbite in winter?
101679.e: Gloves keep the warmth on your hands. Mittens are especially warm.

101680.q: Why do your teeth chatter when you are cold?
101680.e: When we are cold, our muscles shiver very fast. The jaw muscles shiver too, so the teeth chatter.
101680.m: Chattering teeth come from shivering muscles.

101681.q: What is shivering from cold for?
101681.e: Working muscles produce heat. Shivering helps the body to warm up.

101682.q: Which muscles move when your teeth chatter?
101682.e: The jaw muscles open and close the mouth. When they shiver, the teeth knock together.
101682.m: When your teeth chatter, your jaw muscles are shivering.

101683.q: What often appears on the skin at the same time as chattering teeth?
101683.e: When it is cold, the tiny hairs stand up. The skin gets little bumps: goose bumps.
101683.m: When it is cold, you often get goose bumps.

101684.q: What helps when your teeth are chattering with cold?
101684.e: Warm clothes keep heat in the body. Moving about produces extra heat.
101684.m: Warm clothes and moving about help against feeling cold.

101685.q: Can you simply stop shivering from cold on purpose?
101685.e: The body controls shivering by itself. You can hardly stop it by choice.
101685.m: Shivering from cold happens all by itself.

101686.q: When do your teeth often chatter after swimming?
a: When you stand wet in the wind
When you lie in the sun
When you have had a warm shower
101686.e: Wet skin loses a lot of heat through evaporation and wind. Then you quickly get cold.

101687.q: What do chattering teeth tell you?
101687.e: Chattering teeth are a sign that the body is losing too much heat. You should then warm up.
101687.m: Chattering teeth mean your body is cold.

101688.q: What did the Inuit make their snow goggles from in the past?
101688.e: The Inuit carved goggles from wood, bone or antler. Narrow slits let only a little light through.
101688.m: The Inuit carved snow goggles from wood and bone.

101689.q: What did old Inuit snow goggles have instead of lenses?
101689.e: Only a little light gets into the eye through a narrow slit. Even so, people could still see well.
101689.m: Narrow slits let only a little light into the eye.

101690.q: Do you need protective goggles in the snow even when it is cloudy?
a: Yes, the light is still strong
101690.e: A lot of UV radiation gets through clouds too, and the snow reflects it. That is why protection is important even when it is cloudy.
101690.m: Even when it is cloudy, protect your eyes in the snow.

101691.q: What do glacier glasses have at the sides?
101691.e: On glaciers, light comes from all sides. Side shields block this light too.
101691.m: Glacier glasses protect your eyes from the side too.

101692.q: What protects your skin better from UV rays at the beach?
101692.e: Clothes block a large part of the UV rays. Wet skin, on the other hand, does not protect you.
101692.m: Clothes are good protection against UV rays.

101693.q: Who is especially at risk in great heat?
101693.e: Small children and old people are less able to control their body heat. They need extra protection in the heat.
101693.m: Children and old people need special protection in the heat.

101694.q: What is it called when the whole body gets too cold?
101694.e: With hypothermia, the temperature of the whole body drops too far. That is an emergency.
101694.m: When the whole body gets too cold, it is called hypothermia.

101695.q: What helps you sweat less in summer?
101695.e: In the shade, the body heats up less. Then it has less heat to get rid of.
101695.m: You sweat less in the shade.

101696.q: Why do you feel so sticky on muggy days?
a: It is raining on your skin
101696.e: On muggy days, there is already a lot of water in the air. So sweat stays on the skin and does not cool you well.
101696.m: In muggy air, sweat does not cool you well.

101697.q: Which animal sweats a lot when it gallops fast?
101697.e: Horses have many sweat glands in their skin. After running fast, you often see wet fur and white foam.
101697.m: Horses sweat a lot when they work hard.

101698.q: What do many people use against the smell of sweat under the arms?
101698.e: A deodorant reduces the smell under the arms. You put it on clean skin.
101698.m: A deodorant helps against the smell of sweat.

101699.q: What do you do if a friend suddenly becomes confused in the heat and falls over?
a: Get adults and help at once
Go into the sun with them
101699.e: Confusion and passing out in the heat can be signs of heatstroke. Then help is needed at once.
101699.m: In an emergency, get help at once.

101700.q: Why should ski goggles fit tightly against your face?
a: So no wind or snow gets in
So they do not steam up
101700.e: Goggles that fit tightly keep the wind and snowflakes away from your eyes. That way your eyes do not water.
101700.m: Ski goggles fit closely against your face.

101701.q: When do your eyes usually start to hurt after too much sun in the snow?
101701.e: You often only feel the damage from UV rays after a few hours. But by then it is already too late.
101701.m: You often only feel eye damage from the sun later.

101702.q: How does a hat with a wide brim help you in bright light?
101702.e: The brim keeps light from above away from your eyes. That way you need to squint less.
101702.m: A wide hat brim protects against glare.

101703.q: Can you see a clear shadow on a very cloudy day?
101703.e: Clouds spread the light in all directions. That is why there are almost no sharp shadows.
101703.m: With thick clouds, there are hardly any shadows.

101704.q: Should you scratch an itchy chilblain?
101704.e: Scratching can break the delicate skin and make it inflamed. It is better to keep the spot warm and protected.
101704.m: It is better not to scratch chilblains.

101705.q: What is the strong shivering called when a fever is rising?
101705.e: When a fever rises, you feel cold and shiver hard. Your teeth may chatter too.
101705.m: With the chills, you shiver hard even though you have a fever.

101706.q: Why do ski goggles sometimes steam up on the inside?
a: Warm, damp air cools on the lens
101706.e: The air from your face is warm and damp. On the cold lens, it turns into a thin film of water.
101706.m: Warm breath makes cold glass steam up.

101707.q: How does a football fly if you kick it harder?
101707.e: A harder kick gives the ball more energy. That is why it flies off faster.
101707.m: A hard shot makes the ball fast.

101708.q: Which part of your foot do you use for an accurate pass?
101708.e: The inside of the foot is wide and flat. That way you can steer the ball accurately in one direction.
101708.m: Accurate passes are played with the inside of the foot.

101709.q: Which part of your foot do you use for a really hard shot?
101709.e: In an instep shot, the top of the foot hits the ball. That way a lot of energy goes from the leg into the ball.
101709.m: Hard shots are played with the instep.

101710.q: Where do you have to hit the ball so that it flies high into the air?
101710.e: If you hit the ball below its middle, it is lifted upwards. If you hit it on top, it rolls along the ground.
101710.m: Hit the ball low and it goes high.

101711.e: A football is pumped up with air. The air makes it firm and bouncy.
101711.m: A football is filled with air.

101712.q: What happens to a football that has too little air in it?
101712.e: A soft ball soaks up a lot of the energy of the kick without giving it back. It bounces and flies less well.

101713.q: Why does a football hit with spin fly in a curve?
101713.e: A ball that spins fast is pushed to the side by the air. So it flies in a curve.
101713.m: A spinning ball flies in a curve.

101714.q: What slows down a football kicked high in the air?
101714.e: The ball has to push the air in front of it out of the way. That slows it down, and it is called air resistance.
101714.m: The air slows down a flying ball.

101715.q: Roughly how heavy is an adult football?
101715.e: According to the rules, a football weighs between 410 and 450 grams. That is about as much as a small loaf of bread.
101715.m: A football weighs a little less than half a kilogram.

101716.q: Why do you land in sand in the long jump?
a: The sand is a nice yellow
101716.e: Soft sand gives way when you land. That way the landing is gentle and you do not get hurt.

101717.q: Where must you take off at the latest in the long jump?
a: In the middle of the pit
At the start of the runway
101717.e: The take-off board is a board in front of the sandpit. You must not step beyond it.
101717.m: In the long jump you take off at the board.

101718.q: What happens if you step over the board when you take off?
a: You can run up again with no penalty
101718.e: If you step over the board, the jump is invalid. This is called a foul.
101718.m: Stepping over the board makes the jump invalid.

101719.q: Where do you swing your arms when you take off?
101719.e: Swinging your arms forwards and upwards gives you extra momentum. That way you get higher and further.
101719.m: Swinging your arms helps you take off.

101720.q: What pulls a long jumper back to the ground after take-off?
101720.e: The Earth pulls all things towards it. That is why you do not fly for ever but land again.
101720.m: Gravity brings every jumper back down.

101721.q: Roughly how far is the men's world record in the long jump (as of 2026)?
101721.e: In 1991 Mike Powell jumped exactly 8.95 metres. This record has stood for over 30 years.
101721.m: The long jump world record is almost 9 metres.

101722.q: Up to which point in the sand is the jump measured?
a: To the mark closest to the board
To the middle of the pit
To the end of the pit
101722.e: The jump is measured to the mark closest to the board. If you fall backwards, the jump is shorter.
101722.m: In the long jump the mark nearest the board counts.

101723.q: What is the structure that ski jumpers jump from called?
101723.e: A ski jump has an in-run at the top and a steep landing slope at the bottom. The jumper flies in between.
101723.m: Ski jumpers jump from a ski jump.

101724.q: Why do ski jumpers hold their skis in a V shape in the air?
a: So that the skis stay warm
101724.e: With the skis spread apart, the air carries the jumper better. That way they fly longer and further.
101724.m: The V shape helps ski jumpers fly further.

101725.q: What is the landing with one leg slightly in front called?
101725.e: In a telemark landing, one foot is in front of the other. It is safe and earns good marks.
101725.m: The stylish landing in ski jumping is called a telemark.

101726.q: Which Swiss athlete won Olympic gold four times in ski jumping?
101726.e: Simon Ammann won two gold medals in both 2002 and 2010. He is one of the most successful ski jumpers.
101726.m: Simon Ammann is the most famous Swiss ski jumper.

101727.q: Why is the landing slope of a ski jump steep?
a: So that the landing is gentle
So that you can climb up it
101727.e: The slope is about as steep as the flight path. So you do not hit the ground hard but glide on.
101727.m: A steep landing slope makes the landing gentle.

101728.q: What position is a ski jumper in while in the air?
101728.e: The jumper leans far forward over the skis. That way the air carries them.
101728.m: Ski jumpers lean far forward in the air.

101729.q: Why do ski jumpers crouch low on the in-run?
a: The air slows them down less
So that they do not get cold
So that they can see better
101729.e: In a crouch the body is small and compact. So the air slows it down less and you go faster.
101729.m: You go faster in a crouch.

101730.q: What are the biggest ski jumps, where people fly more than 200 metres, called?
101730.e: On ski flying hills the best jumpers fly further than 200 metres. Normal ski jumps are smaller.
101730.m: You fly furthest on ski flying hills.

101731.q: What is the edge from which a ski jumper takes off called?
101731.e: At the end of the in-run comes the take-off table. That is where the jumper pushes off hard.
101731.m: The ski jumper takes off from the take-off table.

101732.q: How does a bobsleigh team start?
a: They push the bob and jump in
It is pulled by a car
101732.e: At the start everyone pushes the bob as fast as they can. Then they jump in one after another.
101732.m: A bob is pushed at the start.

101733.e: The pilot sits right at the front. They steer the bob with two ropes or handles.
101733.m: The pilot at the front steers the bob.

101734.q: What does the brakeman at the back of the bob do after the finish?
101734.e: The brakeman sits at the back. Only after the finish line do they pull the brake.
101734.m: The brakeman brakes the bob after the finish.

101735.q: Why are the bends of a bobsleigh track high and sloping?
a: So that the bob does not fly out
So that spectators can sit on them
101735.e: In a bend, the fast bob wants to keep going straight on. The high sloping wall keeps it on the track.
101735.m: High sloping bends keep the bob on the track.

101736.q: Where is the oldest bobsleigh track in the world?
101736.e: The bobsleigh track from St Moritz to Celerina has existed since 1904. It is the oldest bobsleigh track in the world.
101736.m: The oldest bobsleigh track in the world is in St Moritz.

101737.q: What is special about the bobsleigh track in St Moritz?
a: It is made of natural ice
101737.e: The track is rebuilt every winter from snow and water. It is the only natural ice track for bobs.
101737.m: In St Moritz you ride on natural ice.

101738.q: How fast can a bob go in St Moritz?
101738.e: On the long, steep track a bob reaches up to about 135 kilometres per hour. That is faster than a car is allowed to drive on the motorway.
101738.m: A bob is faster than a car on the motorway.

101739.q: Why do bobsledders wear shoes with spikes at the start?
a: So that they do not slip on the ice
101739.e: Little spikes under the shoes grip the ice. That way the team can push hard.
101739.m: Spikes give a good grip on ice.

101740.q: Roughly how long does a bob run in St Moritz take?
101740.e: The track is about 1700 metres long. A bob only needs about 75 seconds for it.
101740.m: A bob run only takes about a minute.

101741.q: What is an ice hockey puck made of?
101741.e: A puck is made of hard rubber. It is tough and can take hard shots.
101741.m: A puck is made of hard rubber.

101742.e: A puck is flat and round. That way it lies still on the ice and glides well.
101742.m: A puck is a flat disc.

101743.q: Why are pucks chilled in a freezer before a match?
101743.e: Cold rubber is harder and bounces less. The puck then glides more smoothly over the ice.

101744.q: Why does a puck slide much further on ice than on tarmac?
101744.e: On smooth ice there is very little friction. So the puck is hardly slowed down.
101744.m: On smooth ice a puck glides a long way.

101745.q: What do ice hockey players use to shoot the puck?
101745.e: Ice hockey players have a long stick with a flat blade. They use it to move and shoot the puck.
101745.m: You shoot the puck with the stick.

101746.q: Roughly how heavy is a puck?
101746.e: A puck weighs between 156 and 170 grams. That is about as much as an apple.
101746.m: A puck weighs about as much as an apple.

101747.q: What colour is an ice hockey puck?
101747.e: The puck is black. That way it is easy to see on the white ice.
101747.m: The black puck is easy to see on the white ice.

101748.q: How fast can a really hard shot make the puck go?
101748.e: The best players shoot the puck faster than 150 kilometres per hour. That is why goalkeepers wear thick protective kit.
101748.m: A hard shot sends the puck very fast.

101749.q: Which country does hornussen come from?
101749.e: Hornussen is an old Swiss national sport. It is played mainly in the Central Plateau, for example in the canton of Bern.

101750.q: What is the small disc that is hit in hornussen called?
101750.e: The small disc is called the nouss or hornuss. It is hit far up into the air.
101750.m: In hornussen you hit the nouss.

101751.q: Where does hornussen get its name from?
a: The nouss buzzes like a hornet
It is played with a horn
It is only played in autumn
101751.e: The flying nouss makes a buzzing sound. That reminds people of a hornet, which is ‘Hornisse’ in German.
101751.m: The flying nouss buzzes like a hornet.

101752.q: What does the team in the field use to stop the nouss?
101752.e: The paddle (called a ‘Schindel’) is a board with a handle. The players throw it or hold it up high to stop the nouss.
101752.m: The nouss is stopped with the paddle.

101753.q: What does the player use to hit the nouss?
101753.e: The stick is long and bends as it is swung. At the end there is a wooden block that hits the nouss.
101753.m: You hit the nouss with the stick.

101754.q: How fast can a nouss fly?
101754.e: A good strike speeds the nouss up to as much as 300 kilometres per hour. That is why stopping it is hard.
101754.m: A nouss can fly very fast.

101755.q: Roughly how heavy is a nouss?
101755.e: The nouss weighs about 78 grams. It is small and light, which is why it flies so far.
101755.m: A nouss is small and light.

101756.q: Why does the stick in hornussen bend during the strike?
a: It springs and gives more power
101756.e: The flexible stick is loaded like a spring as you swing back. When you strike, it snaps back and gives the nouss a lot of speed.
101756.m: A springy stick hits the nouss a long way.

101757.q: What is the playing field where the nouss is stopped called?
101757.e: The Ries is a long field that gets wider towards the back. The fielders stand there with their paddles.
101757.m: The playing field in hornussen is called the Ries.

101758.q: Where does a Swiss wrestling bout take place?
101758.e: Swiss wrestling takes place in a round area filled with sawdust. It is called the sawdust ring.

101759.q: Why is there sawdust on the ground in Swiss wrestling?
a: It makes the ground as slippery as ice
101759.e: The soft sawdust cushions a fall. That way the wrestlers get hurt less.

101760.q: What do Swiss wrestlers put on over their clothes?
101760.e: Swiss wrestlers wear shorts made of a strong fabric called twill. They grip their opponent by them.
101760.m: Swiss wrestlers wear wrestling shorts made of strong fabric.

101761.q: Why does a Swiss wrestler stand low with legs wide apart?
101761.e: With your legs wide and your body low, you do not tip over so easily. It is hard for the opponent to throw you off balance.
101761.m: Standing wide and low gives good balance.

101762.q: Where do Swiss wrestlers grip each other in a bout?
101762.e: At the start, each wrestler holds the belt and trouser leg of the other's shorts. That way both can pull and lift.
101762.m: Swiss wrestlers hold on to the wrestling shorts.

101763.q: How heavy is the shot in the women's shot put?
101763.e: Women put a shot weighing 4 kilograms. Children and teenagers use lighter shots.

101764.q: Why is it called shot put and not shot throw?
a: You push the shot away from your neck
You throw it with a straight arm from behind your head
101764.e: The shot rests against your neck and is pushed forwards with your arm. Swinging back as in a ball throw is not allowed.
101764.m: In the shot put the shot is pushed away from the neck.

101765.q: Where do you stand in the shot put?
101765.e: The put is made from a circle just over 2 metres across. At the front it has a small board.
101765.m: Shot putters stand in a circle.

101766.q: In which direction is it best to put the shot?
101766.e: If you put it at an angle upwards, the shot flies in a long arc. Straight up or flat, it does not go as far.
101766.m: At an upward angle the shot flies furthest.

101767.q: Why does a shot not fly as far as a tennis ball?
101767.e: A heavy shot needs a lot of force to get fast. With the same force, a light ball gets much faster.
101767.m: Heavy things cannot be thrown as far.

101768.q: Why do some shot putters spin round in the circle before the put?
101768.e: In the rotational technique, the athlete turns round once. This makes the shot faster before they put it.
101768.m: A spin gives the shot more speed.

101769.q: What does the shot leave behind when it lands on the grass?
a: A hole right through the Earth
101769.e: The heavy shot presses a small hollow into the ground. The distance is measured to there.
101769.m: The shot makes a dent in the ground when it lands.

101770.q: What is the string you draw on a bow called?
101770.e: The bowstring joins the two ends of the bow. You pull it back and let it go.
101770.m: The string of a bow is called the bowstring.

101771.q: What stores the energy when you draw a bow?
101771.e: When you draw it, the bow bends more. Like a spring, it wants to go back and shoots the arrow forwards.
101771.m: A drawn bow stores energy like a spring.

101772.q: What are the feathers at the back end of an arrow for?
a: So that the arrow flies straight
So that the arrow is heavier
So that the arrow looks nice
101772.e: The feathers keep the arrow steady in the air. Without them it would wobble.
101772.m: Feathers make an arrow fly straight.

101773.q: What colour is the centre of an archery target?
101773.e: The centre is yellow and is often called the gold. A hit there gives the most points.
101773.m: The centre of the target is yellow.

101774.q: Why do you aim a little higher at a target far away?
a: The arrow drops on the way
The arrow rises on the way
101774.e: Gravity pulls the arrow down during its flight. That is why you aim a little higher at distant targets.

101775.q: How far away is the target in Olympic archery?
101775.e: At the Olympics, archers shoot at 70 metres. The target is 122 centimetres across.

101776.q: What happens if you pull the bowstring back further?
101776.e: The further you pull, the more energy is stored in the bow. This energy passes to the arrow.
101776.m: Drawn further means a faster flight.

101777.q: In the legend, what did William Tell use to shoot the apple off his son's head?
101777.e: Tell used a crossbow, which works like a bow. The string is drawn back with a mechanism.
101777.m: William Tell shot with a crossbow.

101778.q: Why are tennis balls usually bright yellow?
101778.e: Bright yellow stands out well on the court and on TV. That is why the balls were changed from white to yellow.
101778.m: Yellow tennis balls are easy to see.

101779.q: What is inside a tennis ball?
101779.e: A tennis ball is a hollow rubber ball. Inside is air that is squeezed together more than the air outside.
101779.m: A tennis ball is filled with air.

101780.q: What is the outside of a tennis ball covered with?
101780.e: The felt makes the ball a little slower in the air. It also helps the strings grip the ball well.
101780.m: A tennis ball has a felt covering.

101781.q: What happens to a tennis ball that has been used for a long time?
101781.e: Over time air escapes from the ball and the felt wears away. That is why an old ball bounces less well.
101781.m: Old tennis balls bounce less high.

101782.q: How does a tennis ball bounce on a cold day?
101782.e: In the cold the rubber is harder and the air presses less strongly. The ball bounces less high.
101782.m: In the cold, tennis balls bounce less high.

101783.q: What part of a tennis racket works like a little trampoline?
101783.e: The strings give a little when they hit the ball and spring back. That way the ball flies off fast.
101783.m: The strings bounce the ball back.

101784.q: Roughly how heavy is a tennis ball?
101784.e: According to the rules, a tennis ball weighs between 56 and just under 60 grams. That is about as much as an egg.
101784.m: A tennis ball weighs about as much as an egg.

101785.q: Why are new tennis balls sold in airtight tins?
a: So that they keep their pressure
So that they do not smell dirty
101785.e: In the sealed tin, the air inside the balls cannot escape. When you open it you hear a hiss.
101785.m: The tin keeps new tennis balls fresh.

101786.q: How do you lie on the sled in luge?
a: Sitting as if on a chair
101786.e: Luge athletes lie on their backs. Their feet point in the direction of travel.
101786.m: In luge you lie on your back, feet first.

101787.q: What is the sport in which you lie on your tummy, head first, called?
101787.e: In skeleton you lie face down on a flat sled. Your head is at the front.
101787.m: In skeleton you go head first.

101788.q: How do you steer a luge?
a: By pressing with your legs and shoulders
101788.e: The athlete presses with their legs on the front ends of the runners and shifts their shoulders. That makes the luge go in one direction.
101788.m: You steer a luge with your body.

101789.q: Why do luge athletes lie completely flat on the sled?
a: So that the air slows them down less
So that they can see the stars
So that they do not get cold
101789.e: Lying flat, they offer only a small surface to the air. That makes them faster.

101790.q: How fast do luge athletes go in the ice channel?
101790.e: On fast tracks, luge athletes reach well over 120 kilometres per hour. They are among the fastest winter sports athletes.

101791.q: What do luge athletes use to push off on the ice at the start?
101791.e: At the start, the athletes pull themselves forwards on handles. Then they paddle on the ice with their hands; the gloves have little spikes.
101791.m: Luge athletes paddle with their hands at the start.

101792.q: How many people ride on one sled in doubles luge?
101792.e: In doubles, two athletes lie on top of each other on the same sled. The one underneath can hardly see anything.
101792.m: In doubles luge two people ride.

101793.q: What is the track made of in luge?
101793.e: Luge takes place in an ice channel. The smooth ice hardly slows the sled down.
101793.m: Luge athletes ride in a channel of ice.

101794.q: Why do you take a fast run-up in the long jump?
a: The faster, the further the jump
So that you jump more slowly
So that the sand gets warm
101794.e: You take the speed from your run-up into the jump. If you run up fast, you fly further.
101794.m: A fast run-up gives a long jump.

101795.q: In which sport do you run up holding a long pole?
101795.e: In the pole vault you sprint with the pole. Then the pole bends and flings the vaulter upwards.
101795.m: In the pole vault you run up with a pole.

101796.q: In which throw do you run up with the object in your hand?
101796.e: Javelin throwers run up along a long runway. The hammer, discus and shot, on the other hand, are thrown from a circle.
101796.m: In the javelin you take a run-up.

101797.q: How do you run up in the modern high jump?
101797.e: In the high jump you first run straight and then in a curve towards the bar. Then you jump over it backwards.
101797.m: In the high jump you run up in a curve.

101798.q: Where do ski jumpers get their speed from?
a: From going down the in-run track
101798.e: The in-run track is steep. As the jumpers go down it, they get faster and faster.
101798.m: Ski jumpers build up speed on the in-run track.

101799.q: What do long jumpers do so that they hit the take-off spot exactly?
101799.e: Long jumpers count their steps and mark the starting point. That way they hit the take-off board exactly.
101799.m: A measured run-up helps you hit the board.

101800.q: Why doesn't a shot putter take a long run-up?
a: He has to stay inside the circle
101800.e: In the shot put you are not allowed to leave the small circle. That is why a long run-up is impossible.
101800.m: Shot putters stay inside the circle while they throw.

101801.q: Which piece of gym equipment do you jump over after a run-up and a jump onto the springboard?
101801.e: You run up, jump onto the springboard and push off with your hands on the buck. Without a run-up you would not get over it.
101801.m: You need a run-up to vault over the buck.

101802.q: Which group of animals does the earthworm belong to?
101802.e: The earthworm belongs to the segmented worms. Its body is built of many identical sections.
101802.m: The earthworm is a segmented worm.

101803.q: How many legs does an earthworm have?
101803.e: An earthworm has no legs. It moves by making its body long and short.
101803.m: The earthworm crawls with no legs at all.

101804.e: The earthworm is an invertebrate. It has neither bones nor a skeleton made of lime.

101805.q: What colour is the earthworm in the garden usually?
101805.e: The common earthworm is reddish to brown. That way it hardly stands out in the soil.
101805.m: The earthworm is usually reddish brown.

101806.q: What does the earthworm swallow along with plant remains?
101806.e: The earthworm eats its way through the ground and swallows a lot of soil as it goes. It digests the fine plant remains from the soil.

101807.q: What does the earthworm leave behind as small crumbs on the soil?
101807.e: The earthworm's little piles of droppings are very fertile. They contain lots of nutrients for plants.
101807.m: Earthworm droppings are a good fertiliser.

101808.q: What gets into the ground through the earthworms' tunnels?
101808.e: The many tunnels loosen the soil. That way air and rainwater get deep into the ground.
101808.m: Earthworm tunnels bring air and water into the ground.

101809.q: Which garden bird often pulls earthworms out of the lawn?
101809.e: The blackbird hops across the lawn and pulls earthworms out of the soil. It also feeds its young with them.

101810.q: What happens to an earthworm that lies in the blazing sun for a long time?
101810.e: The earthworm needs damp surroundings. In the sun its skin dries out and it dies.
101810.m: The earthworm cannot cope with dryness.

101811.e: Humus is an important part of the soil. It makes the soil fertile and loose.

101812.e: Humus is very dark. The more humus a soil has, the darker it is.
101812.m: Humus is dark brown to black.

101813.q: In which layer of soil do you find the most humus?
101813.e: Plant remains fall onto the ground from above. That is why the top layer of soil is richest in humus.
101813.m: Most humus lies in the top layer of soil.

101814.q: What can humus store especially well?
101814.e: Humus soaks up water like a sponge. That way plants have water for longer, even in dry spells.
101814.m: Humus stores water like a sponge.

101815.q: Why do plants grow especially well in humus?
a: It has no living things in it
101815.e: Humus holds lots of nutrients from rotted plants. The roots of new plants take them up.

101816.q: Which animals help old leaves turn into humus?
101816.e: Earthworms eat fallen leaves and mix them with soil. Their droppings become fertile humus.

101817.q: How fast does a thick layer of humus form in the forest?
101817.e: Humus forms only slowly. Nature needs many years for a thick layer.

101818.q: What forms on the compost heap from garden and kitchen waste?
101818.e: Plant remains rot on the compost heap. Over time they turn into dark, crumbly soil.
101818.m: Plant waste turns into soil on the compost heap.

101819.q: What can go on the compost heap?
101819.e: Potato peel is plant waste and rots. Plastic, glass and batteries do not belong on the compost heap.
101819.m: Vegetable peelings belong on the compost heap.

101820.q: What does NOT belong on the compost heap?
101820.e: Plastic does not rot. It stays in the compost and pollutes the soil.
101820.m: Plastic never belongs on the compost heap.

101821.q: Why is it better not to put cooked meat scraps on the garden compost heap?
101821.e: Meat scraps smell strongly and attract rats and other animals. That is why they are left out of the garden compost.
101821.m: Meat scraps do not belong on the garden compost heap.

101822.q: What is finished compost used for in the garden?
101822.e: Mature compost contains lots of nutrients. It is mixed into the beds so that plants grow well.

101823.q: What does good, finished compost smell like?
101823.e: Mature compost smells pleasantly earthy. If a compost heap stinks, it is often too wet.
101823.m: Good compost smells of the forest floor.

101824.q: Which tiny helpers break down the waste in the compost?
101824.e: Invisibly small bacteria and fungi break down the plant remains. Worms and woodlice help too.
101824.m: Bacteria and fungi turn waste into compost.

101825.q: Roughly how long does it take for compost to be ready?
a: A few months to a year
101825.e: Plant remains rot in the compost over several months. Mature compost is often ready after about a year.
101825.m: Compost takes months to be ready.

101826.q: Can coffee grounds go on the compost heap?
a: No, they drive the worms away
101826.e: Coffee grounds are plant waste and rot well. Earthworms even like them.
101826.m: Coffee grounds can go on the compost heap.

101827.q: Where is the best place to put a compost heap?
101827.e: In partial shade the compost does not dry out and does not get too wet. That way the creatures in the soil work well.
101827.m: A compost heap is best placed in partial shade.

101828.q: What should a compost heap stand on?
101828.e: If the compost stands on bare soil, earthworms and other creatures can move in. Extra water can also drain away.
101828.m: A compost heap needs contact with the soil.

101829.q: What do you put right at the bottom of a new compost heap?
101829.e: Coarse twigs at the bottom let air into the heap. Water can also drain away better.
101829.m: Coarse twigs go right at the bottom of the compost heap.

101830.q: What does the inside of a compost heap often feel like when it is working well?
101830.e: When the tiny creatures break down the waste, heat is produced. That is why a fresh compost heap gets warm inside.
101830.m: A working compost heap gets warm inside.

101831.q: How damp should a compost heap be?
101831.e: The creatures in the compost need moisture. But if it is too wet, there is no air and it starts to stink.
101831.m: A compost heap should be damp but not wet.

101832.q: Why do you turn a compost heap every now and then?
101832.e: Turning loosens and mixes the compost. That way the creatures get fresh air.
101832.m: Turning brings air into the compost heap.

101833.q: Which prickly animal likes to shelter by a compost heap?
101833.e: The hedgehog finds warmth in the compost heap and lots of insects and worms to eat. That is why it likes visiting compost heaps.
101833.m: The hedgehog likes visiting the compost heap.

101834.q: Why do you chop up big branches before they go on the compost heap?
101834.e: Small pieces have a lot of surface. Fungi and bacteria can get to work on them better there.

101835.q: What helps with a wet, smelly compost heap?
101835.e: Dry material such as leaves or wood chips soaks up the wet. At the same time air gets back into the heap.
101835.m: Dry material loosens up a wet compost heap again.

101836.q: What does it mean when leaves rot?
a: They slowly break down into soil
101836.e: When rotting, the leaves break down into tiny pieces. In the end they become soil.

101837.q: What do fungi and bacteria need so that leaves rot quickly?
101837.e: The tiny decomposers need water to live. In dry leaves rotting is only slow.
101837.m: Leaves rot faster when they are damp.

101838.q: When do leaves rot especially slowly?
a: When there are lots of worms
101838.e: In the cold the tiny creatures hardly work. That is why leaves rot very slowly in winter.

101839.q: Which turns into soil faster: soft leaves or a thick branch?
101839.e: Soft leaves break down quickly. A thick branch is hard and takes many years to rot.
101839.m: Soft leaves rot faster than wood.

101840.q: What happens to a banana skin that you put in the compost?
a: It turns brown and breaks down
It gets as hard as wood
101840.e: Bacteria and fungi break down the skin. It first turns brown and then falls apart.
101840.m: A banana skin rots in the compost.

101841.q: What does not rot in nature at all, or only after a very long time?
101841.e: Glass is not broken down by bacteria and fungi. It stays in nature for a very long time.

101842.q: What do you often see on a leaf that has been lying on the ground for a long time?
a: Only the fine network of veins
101842.e: Small creatures first eat the soft leaf tissue. The hard leaf veins are left over for longer.
101842.m: Often only the veins are left of old leaves.

101843.q: Who helps with rotting by eating leaves into small pieces?
101843.e: Woodlice, millipedes and worms break up the leaves. After that fungi and bacteria can break them down further.
101843.m: Soil creatures break up the leaves.

101844.q: What lives in a handful of garden soil?
101844.e: Billions of tiny living things live in a handful of healthy soil. Most of them can only be seen with a microscope.
101844.m: Countless living things live in garden soil.

101845.q: What does the garden soil in the bed need when it has not rained for a long time?
101845.e: Without rain the soil gets dry and hard. Then you water the beds so the plants don't wilt.

101846.q: What do you use to loosen the garden soil in the bed?
101846.e: The soil is loosened with a garden fork or spade. That way the roots can grow more easily.
101846.m: The garden fork loosens the soil.

101847.q: What do lots of earthworms in the garden soil show?
a: That the soil is too dry
101847.e: Earthworms only live in large numbers where the soil is loose, damp and rich in food. That is why lots of worms are a sign of healthy soil.
101847.m: Lots of earthworms show healthy garden soil.

101848.q: What does good garden soil feel like?
101848.e: Good garden soil falls apart into small crumbs. You can easily crumble it with your fingers.
101848.m: Good garden soil is loose and crumbly.

101849.q: Why shouldn't you walk around on freshly loosened beds?
101849.e: Stepping on it makes the loose soil firm again. Then air, water and roots get through less well.
101849.m: You don't walk around on beds.

101850.q: What is often mixed into garden soil to make it more fertile?
101850.e: Compost brings humus and nutrients into the soil. That way vegetables and flowers grow better.
101850.m: Compost makes garden soil more fertile.

101851.q: Apart from crumbs of soil, what else is in good garden soil?
101851.e: Between the crumbs there are lots of small gaps. They hold air and water for roots and soil creatures.
101851.m: There is air and water in good soil.

101852.q: What is the heap of earth a mole throws up in the garden called?
101852.e: The mole digs tunnels under the ground. It pushes the loose earth upwards, and so a molehill forms.

a: Lots of small grains of rock
101853.e: Sand is made of small grains of rock. They are often grains of the mineral quartz.
101853.m: Sand is made of small grains of rock.

101854.e: Wind, water, frost and heat break up rock. Over a long time small grains of sand form from it.

101855.q: What happens when you pour water on sand?
a: It stays standing for a long time
101855.e: There are big gaps between the grains of sand. The water flows down quickly through these gaps.
101855.m: Water soaks away quickly in sand.

101856.q: Why does sandy soil dry out quickly in summer?
101856.e: Sand can hardly hold on to water. That is why sandy soil soon gets dry again after rain.

101857.q: What does sand feel like between your fingers?
101857.e: You can feel the separate hard grains. That is why sand feels rough and gritty.

101858.q: When is the best time to build a castle in the sandpit?
a: When the sand is completely dry
101858.e: Damp sand sticks together a little. Dry sand, on the other hand, trickles apart.
101858.m: You can build castles with damp sand.

101859.q: What is made from sand when it is heated very strongly?
101859.e: When quartz sand is heated very strongly with other substances, it melts. Glass is made from it.

101860.q: What trickles from top to bottom in an hourglass?
101860.e: In an hourglass, fine sand trickles through a narrow gap. This lets you measure a certain amount of time.
101860.m: An hourglass measures time with trickling sand.

101861.q: What happens to clay soil when it dries out completely?
101861.e: As it dries, clay soil loses water and shrinks. It gets hard and cracks.
101861.m: Dry clay soil gets hard and cracked.

101862.q: What often stays for a long time on clay soil after heavy rain?
101862.e: Clay soil lets water through only slowly. That is why puddles form easily on clay soil.
101862.m: Puddles often stay on clay soil.

101863.q: What did people build from clay in the past?
101863.e: Clay was used for building thousands of years ago. People made walls and whole houses from it.
101863.m: People built houses from clay long ago.

101864.q: What is made from clay in the kiln?
101864.e: Clay is shaped and fired in the kiln. This makes hard bricks and tiles for roofs and walls.
101864.m: Bricks and tiles are fired from clay.

101865.q: What can you easily roll between your hands from damp clay?
101865.e: Clay can be shaped and holds together. That is why you can roll it into a sausage, but not sand.
101865.m: You can roll clay into a sausage.

101866.q: Why is clay soil often hard to dig?
101866.e: Clay has very fine particles that stick tightly together. That is why it is heavy and dense.
101866.m: Clay soil is hard to dig.

101867.q: What does clay soil hold on to better than sandy soil?
101867.e: The fine clay particles hold on to water well. That is why plants have water for longer in clay soil.

101868.q: Which group of animals do the woodlice in the garden belong to?
101868.e: Woodlice are related to crabs. They are among the few crustaceans that live on land.
101868.m: Woodlice are crustaceans that live on land.

101869.q: How many legs does an adult woodlouse have?
101869.e: Adult woodlice have seven pairs of legs. That makes 14 legs in all.

101870.q: Where do you especially often find woodlice?
101870.e: Woodlice need moisture, otherwise they dry out. That is why they hide under stones, wood and leaves.
101870.m: Woodlice live in damp, dark places.

101871.e: Woodlice eat dead leaves and wood. In this way they help new soil to form.

101872.q: What does a pill woodlouse do when it feels threatened?
a: It rolls up into a ball
101872.e: The pill woodlouse can roll itself up into a ball. Its hard armour then protects it.
101872.m: The pill woodlouse rolls into a ball when in danger.

101873.q: What happens to a woodlouse if it lies in the hot sun for a long time?
101873.e: Woodlice need moisture. In the hot sun they dry out, which is why they hide in damp, dark places.
101873.m: Woodlice dry out in the sun.

101874.q: What colour are common woodlice usually?
101874.e: Common woodlice are usually grey to greyish brown. This keeps them well camouflaged under stones.

101875.e: The woodlouse's back is covered with plates. This armour protects the animal.

101876.q: What is manure on a farm made of?
101876.e: Manure is a mixture of animal droppings and straw from the stable. The straw is used as bedding for the animals.
101876.m: Manure is made of animal droppings and straw.

101877.q: What do farmers use manure for?
101877.e: Manure contains lots of nutrients. On the field it helps plants to grow well.
101877.m: Manure is a fertiliser for the fields.

101878.q: Why does a manure heap steam on cold days?
101878.e: Inside the manure, tiny living things break down the droppings and straw. This produces heat, which you can see as steam.
101878.m: A manure heap is warm inside.

101879.q: Which tool do you use to load manure onto a wheelbarrow by hand?
101879.e: A pitchfork has long, pointed prongs. You can use it to pick up loose manure easily.
101879.m: You load manure with a pitchfork.

101880.q: Which beetle makes balls out of dung?
101880.e: The dung roller is a dung beetle. It shapes dung into balls and rolls them away.
101880.m: The dung roller beetle rolls balls of dung.

101881.q: Why shouldn't you put fresh manure straight onto young plants?
101881.e: Fresh manure contains a lot of harsh substances. Young roots can be damaged by them, so it is left to rot down well first.
101881.m: Manure should be well rotted before it goes on the bed.

101882.q: Which animal does the manure gardeners often use for roses come from?
101882.e: Horse manure is very popular with gardeners. It is loose and works well for roses and flower beds.
101882.m: Horse manure is a popular garden fertiliser.

101883.q: Which insects often buzz around a manure heap in summer?
101883.e: Flies are attracted by the smell of manure. Many also lay their eggs in it.

101884.q: What is mulch in the garden?
101884.e: Mulch is a covering of plant remains on the soil. You can use grass cuttings, leaves or bark, for example.
101884.m: Mulch is a blanket for the garden soil.

101885.q: What does mulch do with the moisture in the soil?
101885.e: The layer of mulch protects the soil from sun and wind. That way less water evaporates.

101886.q: Why do fewer weeds grow under a layer of mulch?
101886.e: The layer of mulch covers the soil. Small weed seedlings therefore get hardly any light.

101887.q: What often lies as a brown layer under the bushes in parks?
101887.e: Bark mulch is made of shredded tree bark. You often see it under bushes.
101887.m: Bark mulch is made of tree bark.

101888.q: What happens to a layer of leaf mulch over time?
101888.e: Soil animals and fungi slowly break the mulch down. This turns into new humus for the soil.
101888.m: Over time, mulch turns into humus.

101889.q: Why do you only spread fresh grass cuttings thinly as mulch?
a: Otherwise it gets as hard as wood
101889.e: Fresh grass cuttings are very wet. In thick layers there is no air, and they start to rot and smell.
101889.m: Use grass cuttings only thinly as mulch.

101890.q: How does mulch help the soil on hot summer days?
101890.e: Mulch works like a sunshade for the soil. The earth underneath stays cooler.
101890.m: Mulch protects the soil from heat.

101891.q: Which animals like to work under a layer of mulch?
101891.e: Under the mulch it is damp and there is food. That is why earthworms feel at home there.

101892.q: What does the green waste collection pick up in many Swiss municipalities?
101892.e: For the green waste collection, the municipality picks up green waste. This includes plant remains from the garden and kitchen.
101892.m: The green waste collection picks up green waste.

101894.q: What goes in the green waste bin?
101894.e: Grass cuttings are plant remains and count as green waste. Aluminium, PET and clothes are collected separately.
101894.m: Grass cuttings go in the green waste.

101895.q: What does NOT belong in the green waste?
101895.e: Cat litter with droppings belongs in the rubbish bag. In the green waste it would contaminate the composting plant.
101895.m: Cat litter goes in the rubbish.

101896.q: Where is green waste taken after it is collected?
101896.e: Green waste goes to a composting or fermentation plant. There it is turned into compost.
101896.m: Green waste becomes compost in a plant.

101897.q: Which gas can be produced from green waste in a fermentation plant?
101897.e: In a fermentation plant, bacteria break down green waste without air. This produces biogas, which provides energy.
101897.m: Biogas can be made from green waste.

101898.q: What is good about collecting green waste separately?
101898.e: Green waste collected separately can be composted. That way the nutrients go back into the soil.
101898.m: Green waste turns back into fertile soil.

101899.q: When is there especially a lot of green waste in many municipalities?
a: In autumn, when the leaves fall
101899.e: In autumn lots of leaves fall from the trees. On top of that there are leftovers from the vegetable garden.
101899.m: There is lots of green waste in autumn.

101990.q: What do you call relaxed, easy running as a sport?
101990.e: When you jog, you run easily and not very fast. That way you can run for a long time.

101991.q: Which shoes are best to wear for jogging?
101991.e: Running shoes are light and cushion every step. That protects your feet and knees.
101991.m: For jogging, wear good running shoes.

101992.q: How can you tell that you are not running too fast when jogging?
101992.e: If you can still chat while jogging, you are running at the right speed. That way you can keep going for a long time.
101992.m: When jogging, you should still be able to talk.

101993.q: Which surface is especially gentle on your joints when jogging?
101993.e: A woodland path cushions your steps a little. That is gentle on your feet, knees and joints.
101993.m: Jogging on soft woodland paths is gentle on your joints.

101994.q: What is a running race of about 42 kilometres called?
101994.e: A marathon is exactly 42.195 kilometres long. In Switzerland, for example, there are marathons in Zurich and Lucerne.
101994.m: A marathon is about 42 kilometres long.

101995.q: What is a running trail in the woods with exercise stations called in Switzerland?
101995.e: On the Vitaparcours, you jog through the woods. At the stations, you do exercises such as jumping or pull-ups.
101995.m: On the Vitaparcours, you jog and exercise in the woods.

101996.q: Roughly how many kilometres long is a half marathon?
101996.e: A half marathon is exactly 21.0975 kilometres long. That is half the marathon distance.
101996.m: A half marathon is about 21 kilometres long.

101997.q: What do you wear when you go jogging at dusk?
101997.e: A high-visibility vest shines brightly in car headlights. That way you can be seen from far away.
101997.m: In the dark, a high-visibility vest makes you visible.

101998.q: What do you wear on your head for protection when cycling?
101998.e: A bike helmet protects your head if you fall. It must fit well and be fastened firmly.
101998.m: When cycling, a helmet protects your head.

101999.q: What do you use to brake on a bike?
101999.e: The brake levers are on the handlebars. When you pull them, the wheels slow down.
101999.m: On a bike, you brake with the brake levers.

102000.q: What do you signal with your outstretched arm when cycling?
102000.e: With your arm stretched out, you show which way you are turning. That way others know what you are about to do.
102000.m: Before turning, you stretch out your arm.

102001.q: Which test for road safety do many Swiss schoolchildren take?
102001.e: In many cantons, children take the cycling test at primary school. They show that they know the rules of the road.
102001.m: Through the cycling test, children learn the rules of the road.

102002.q: What must light up on a bike when it is dark?
102002.e: A white light shines at the front and a red light at the back. That way everyone else in traffic can see you.
102002.m: In the dark, a bike needs lights at the front and back.

102003.q: Which parts of the body work hardest when cycling?
102003.e: When you push the pedals, it is mainly the muscles in your legs that work. That makes your legs strong.

102004.q: Which side of the road do you cycle on in Switzerland?
102004.e: In Switzerland, traffic drives on the right. Bikes ride on the right-hand edge of the road.
102004.m: In Switzerland, you ride on the right.

102005.q: What do you use on a bike to make others notice you?
102005.e: You ring the bell so that others can hear you. That is important with pedestrians, for example.
102005.m: You warn others with the bell.

102006.q: In which swimming stroke do you lie on your back?
102006.e: In backstroke, you lie on your back. Your face looks up out of the water.
102006.m: In backstroke, you lie on your back.

102007.q: Which swimming stroke is also named after an insect?
102007.e: The dolphin stroke is also called butterfly. Both arms swing over the water at the same time.

102008.q: Which organisation publishes the well-known water safety rules in Switzerland?
102008.e: The SLRG is the Swiss Lifesaving Society. Its water safety rules help prevent accidents in the water.
102008.m: In Switzerland, the SLRG publishes the water safety rules.

102009.q: What does a water safety rule say about murky, unfamiliar water?
a: Take a run-up and jump in
Jump in with your eyes closed
102009.e: In murky water, you cannot see whether there are stones or branches in it. That is why you should not jump in.
102009.m: Do not jump into unfamiliar water.

102010.q: What helps small children who cannot swim yet in the water?
102010.e: Armbands are filled with air and help children stay afloat. Even so, an adult must always keep watch.
102010.m: Small children need help and supervision in the water.

102011.q: Why do you not run along the edge of the pool at the swimming baths?
102011.e: The floor by the pool is wet and smooth. If you run, you can slip and hurt yourself.
102011.m: Walk slowly on the wet poolside.

102012.q: How long is an Olympic swimming pool?
102012.e: At the Olympic Games, swimmers race in a 50-metre pool. Many indoor pools have shorter 25-metre pools.
102012.m: An Olympic pool is 50 metres long.

102013.q: What is the person who keeps an eye on swimmers at the swimming pool called?
102013.e: The lifeguard makes sure nobody gets into danger. They can help if someone has problems in the water.
102013.m: At the swimming pool, the lifeguard keeps watch.
