102014.q: What do you wear around your hips and legs when rope climbing?
102014.e: The rope is knotted onto the climbing harness. The harness holds you if you fall onto the rope.
102014.m: When climbing, you wear a climbing harness.

102015.q: What is climbing without a rope on low walls above thick mats called?
102015.e: When bouldering, you only climb so high that you can jump down onto the mat. That is why you do not need a rope.
102015.m: Bouldering is climbing without a rope at jumping height.

102016.q: What holds you if you slip while climbing on a high wall?
102016.e: The rope is fastened to your harness. It catches you if you slip.
102016.m: When climbing high, the rope holds you.

102017.q: What does the person standing at the bottom holding the rope do when you climb?
102017.e: This person is called the belayer. They hold the rope and brake if you fall.
102017.m: The belayer holds the rope when you climb.

102018.q: Why do climbers rub white powder on their hands?
102018.e: The powder is called chalk (magnesium carbonate). It makes your hands dry, so you slip less.
102018.m: Chalk keeps your hands dry when climbing.

102019.q: In which city was sport climbing part of the Olympic Games for the first time?
102019.e: Sport climbing became an Olympic sport for the first time at the Tokyo Summer Games. The Games took place in 2021.
102019.m: Sport climbing became Olympic in Tokyo.

102020.q: What does a helmet protect you from when climbing on rock?
102020.e: On rock, stones can come loose and fall down. The helmet then protects your head.
102020.m: On rock, a helmet protects you from stones.

102021.e: Climbing shoes fit tightly on your foot. The rubber sole grips well on small footholds.
102021.m: Climbing shoes are tight and have a grippy sole.

102022.q: On which piece of gym equipment do you bounce up on a stretched sheet?
102022.e: A trampoline has a jumping bed that hangs on springs. It throws you upwards.
102022.m: You bounce high on a trampoline.

102023.q: What is the exercise called where you roll forwards over your head?
102023.e: In a forward roll, you curl up round like a ball. Then you roll over your back.
102023.m: In a forward roll, you curl up round.

102024.q: Which piece of gym equipment hangs from the ceiling on two ropes?
102024.e: The rings hang freely from the ceiling. You hold on to them and swing or hang.
102024.m: On the rings, you hang and swing.

102025.q: What do you stand on when you do a handstand?
102025.e: In a handstand, you support yourself on your hands. Your legs point straight up.
102025.m: In a handstand, you stand on your hands.

102026.q: What is put under gym equipment so that you land softly?
102026.e: Gym mats are thick and soft. They protect you when you fall or land.

102027.q: What is the balance beam for?
102027.e: The balance beam is a narrow beam. You practise your balance on it.
102027.m: On the balance beam, you practise balance.

102028.q: What is the big Swiss gymnastics festival that takes place about every six years called?
102028.e: At the Federal Gymnastics Festival, many thousands of gymnasts meet. In 2025 it took place in Lausanne.
102028.m: The Federal Gymnastics Festival is the biggest gymnastics festival in Switzerland.

102029.q: In which exercise do you turn sideways over your hands and feet?
102029.e: In a cartwheel, you put your hands down first and then your feet. You turn to the side like a wheel.
102029.m: In a cartwheel, you turn sideways.

102030.q: In which exercise do you lie on your back and stretch your legs straight up?
102030.e: In the candlestick, you support your back with your hands. Your legs point straight up like a candle.
102030.m: In the candlestick, your legs point upwards.

102031.q: How many players does a football team have on the pitch?
102031.e: A team has eleven players on the pitch. One of them is the goalkeeper.
102031.m: In football, eleven players play per team.

102032.q: Who may catch the ball with their hands in football?
102032.e: Only the goalkeeper may touch the ball with their hands. That only applies inside their penalty area.
102032.m: Only the goalkeeper may use their hands.

102033.q: How long does a normal adult football match last?
102033.e: A match has two halves of 45 minutes each. Together that makes 90 minutes.

102034.q: Which card does the referee show to send a player off?
102034.e: For a serious foul, the referee shows the red card. The player then has to leave the pitch.
102034.m: With a red card, you have to leave the pitch.

102035.q: What does the yellow card mean in football?
102035.e: The yellow card is a caution. Anyone who gets two yellow cards in the same match has to leave the pitch.
102035.m: The yellow card is a caution.

102036.q: What is the Swiss national football team often called for short?
102036.e: The Swiss call their national team “Nati” for short. It plays in red shirts.
102036.m: The Swiss national team is called the Nati for short.

102038.q: In which Swiss city does the world football association FIFA have its headquarters?
102038.e: FIFA has its headquarters in Zurich. It organises the Football World Cup, for example.

102039.q: What is the hopping game with boxes drawn on the ground called?
102039.e: In hopscotch, you hop on one leg through the boxes. First you throw a stone into one of the squares.
102039.m: In hopscotch, you hop through boxes.

102040.q: What do you use to draw game courts on the playground?
102040.e: Pavement chalk is thick and colourful. You can draw on tarmac with it, and the rain washes it away again.
102040.m: You draw on the ground with pavement chalk.

102041.q: What is the game called where everyone hides and one child looks for them?
102041.e: In hide-and-seek, one child counts with their eyes closed. Then they look for the others.
102041.m: In hide-and-seek, one child looks for the others.

102042.q: In which game does a rope swing over your head and under your feet?
102042.e: When skipping, you jump over the rope each time. That trains stamina and skill.
102042.m: When skipping, you jump over the rope.

102043.q: On which piece of playground equipment do you whizz from the top to the bottom sitting down?
102043.e: On the slide, you climb up a ladder. Then you slide down the smooth chute.
102043.m: On the slide, you slide down.

102044.q: In which game do you jump over a stretched elastic band?
102044.e: In French skipping, two children hold the elastic stretched with their legs. A third child jumps in and out following the rules.
102044.m: In French skipping, you jump over an elastic band.

102045.q: On which piece of playground equipment do two children go up and down?
102045.e: On the seesaw, one child sits at each end. In Switzerland, it is often also called “Gigampfi”.
102045.m: On the seesaw, you go up and down.

102046.q: What gets warm and loose when you warm up?
102046.e: Moving makes more blood flow into the muscles. That makes them warm and loose.
102046.m: When you warm up, your muscles get warm.

102047.q: What is a good warm-up exercise?
a: Sitting still for a long time
102047.e: Easy running and hopping slowly get the body going. After that, you can get faster and stronger.
102047.m: To warm up, you first move gently.

102048.q: Roughly how long does a warm-up in school PE last?
102048.e: A warm-up usually lasts about 10 to 15 minutes. That is enough for the body to be ready.
102048.m: A warm-up lasts about ten minutes.

102049.q: What happens to your pulse when you warm up?
102049.e: Your pulse shows how fast your heart is beating. When you warm up, it slowly gets faster.
102049.m: When you warm up, your pulse rises slowly.

102050.q: What do you call slow running after training?
102050.e: When cooling down, the body calms down again. Pulse and breathing slowly become calmer.
102050.m: After sport, you cool down with slow running.

102051.q: In which exercise do you jump and clap your hands together above your head?
102051.e: In star jumps, you jump your legs apart and back together again. At the same time, your arms go up and down.
102051.m: Star jumps are a good warm-up exercise.

102052.q: Which exercise loosens your shoulders when you warm up?
102052.e: In arm circles, your arms turn in big circles. Your shoulder joints move as you do this.

102053.q: Where do PE lessons take place when it rains?
102053.e: The sports hall is a big room for sport. You can do gym and play games there in any weather.
102053.m: When it rains, PE is in the sports hall.

102054.q: At least how many PE lessons per week does the Swiss federal government require for compulsory school (not including kindergarten)?
102054.e: The Swiss Sport Promotion Act requires at least three PE lessons per week. This rule does not apply to kindergarten.
102054.m: In Swiss schools, there are at least three PE lessons per week.

102055.q: Which shoes do you wear in the sports hall?
102055.e: Trainers with light-coloured soles do not leave black marks on the hall floor. They do not slip either.
102055.m: In the sports hall, you wear clean trainers.

102056.q: In which ball game do you throw the ball into a basket?
102056.e: In basketball, the basket hangs high on a board. If you throw the ball in, you score points.
102056.m: In basketball, you shoot at a basket.

102057.q: In which game do you try to hit opponents with a ball?
102057.e: In dodgeball, there are two courts. Anyone hit by the ball has to leave the court.
102057.m: In dodgeball, you hit opponents with the ball.

102058.q: What is the day called when the whole school does competitions outdoors?
102058.e: On sports day, there are races, jumps, throws and games. Often all classes take part.
102058.m: On sports day, all classes do competitions.

102059.q: Where do you land in the long jump?
102059.e: In the long jump, you jump into a pit of sand. The distance is measured to the mark you make.
102059.m: In the long jump, you land in sand.

102060.e: In a sprint, you run as fast as you can. The distance is short, for example 60 or 80 metres.
102060.m: A sprint is a short, fast run.

102061.q: What do you hold in your hands when skiing?
102061.e: Ski poles help with balance and pushing off. You also use them when turning.
102061.m: When skiing, you hold ski poles.

102062.q: What protects your eyes from wind and snow when skiing?
102062.e: Ski goggles fit closely around your eyes. They protect against wind, snow and bright light.

102063.q: What is a ski race called where you ski tightly around lots of gates?
102063.e: In slalom, the gates are close together. You have to make lots of quick turns.
102063.m: In slalom, you ski around lots of gates.

102064.q: How do you get comfortably up the mountain when skiing?
102064.e: Ski lifts and chairlifts pull or carry you uphill. Then you ski down.
102064.m: The ski lift takes you uphill.

102065.q: Which Swiss skier won the overall World Cup in alpine skiing several times in a row from 2022?
102065.e: Marco Odermatt from Nidwalden won the overall World Cup every year from 2022 to 2026, so five times in a row (as of 2026). He is one of the best skiers in the world.
102065.m: Marco Odermatt is a Swiss ski star.

102066.q: How do beginners position their skis to brake?
102066.e: In a snowplough, the ski tips point towards each other and the ends point apart. That slows you down.

102067.q: What colour are the easiest ski runs in Switzerland?
102067.e: In Switzerland, easy runs are blue. Intermediate runs are marked red and difficult ones black.

102068.q: Why do you need sun cream in the snow, even in winter?
a: The sun is bigger in winter
102068.e: Snow strongly reflects sunlight. That is why you quickly get sunburnt in the mountains.
102068.m: In the snow, you need sun protection.

102069.q: Where does the famous Lauberhorn race take place?
102069.e: The Lauberhorn race is one of the longest downhill races in the World Cup. It takes place every January in Wengen in the Bernese Oberland.
102069.m: The Lauberhorn race is in Wengen.

102070.q: What colour are normal hiking signposts in Switzerland?
102070.e: Swiss hiking trails are marked with yellow signposts. They show destinations and times.

102071.q: What colours are the markings of a mountain hiking trail?
102071.e: Mountain hiking trails are marked white-red-white. They are steeper and more difficult than normal hiking trails.
102071.m: Mountain hiking trails are marked white-red-white.

102072.q: Which shoes do you wear when hiking in the mountains?
102072.e: Walking boots have a thick sole with tread. They give good grip on stony paths.
102072.m: In the mountains, you wear walking boots.

102073.q: What is the food you take with you on a hike called?
102073.e: Provisions are food for the journey, for example bread, cheese and fruit. You carry them in your rucksack.
102073.m: Provisions are food for the journey.

102074.q: What does the time on a Swiss hiking signpost show?
a: Roughly how long you will walk
102074.e: The signposts show roughly how many hours and minutes you need to reach the destination. That way you can plan the hike.
102074.m: The signpost shows the approximate walking time.

102075.q: What do you do with your rubbish on a hike?
a: I take it back with me
I throw it in the stream
102075.e: Rubbish harms nature and animals. That is why you pack it up and throw it away at home.
102075.m: Take your rubbish back home with you.

102076.q: Why do you take a jacket on a mountain hike, even on a sunny day?
a: Because the weather in the mountains changes quickly
Because you walk faster in a jacket
Because you have to sit on it
Because otherwise the rucksack is empty
102076.e: In the mountains, it can quickly become cool, windy or rainy. With a jacket, you are prepared for that.
102076.m: In the mountains, the weather changes quickly.

102077.q: What do many families in Switzerland do at a fireplace when hiking?
102077.e: In Switzerland, grilling something over an open fire is called “bräteln”. Cervelat sausages on a stick are popular.
102077.m: On a hike, people like to grill a sausage.

102078.q: What do you carry your drinks and rain jacket in when hiking?
102078.e: A rucksack is carried on your back. That way you have both hands free.
102078.m: When hiking, you carry a rucksack.

102079.q: What does stamina mean in sport?
a: Being able to keep going for a long time
Being able to jump very high
Being able to lift very heavy things
Being able to aim very well
102079.e: If you have stamina, you can keep moving for a long time without getting tired quickly. For example, when running a long way.
102079.m: Stamina means being able to keep going for a long time.

102080.q: Which sport is a typical endurance sport?
102080.e: In cross-country skiing, you move for a long time without a break. You need a lot of stamina for it.
102080.m: Cross-country skiing is an endurance sport.

102081.q: Which organs get stronger through endurance training?
102081.e: If you regularly run, swim or cycle, you train your heart and lungs. They then work better.
102081.m: Endurance training strengthens your heart and lungs.

102082.q: What is the big cycle race through Switzerland that lasts several days called?
102082.e: The Tour de Suisse is a stage race for professional cyclists. The riders need a lot of stamina for it.
102082.m: The Tour de Suisse is a cycle race through Switzerland.

102083.q: Which three sports do you do one after another in a triathlon?
102083.e: In a triathlon, you swim first, then cycle, and finally run. That takes a lot of stamina.
102083.m: A triathlon is made up of swimming, cycling and running.

102084.q: What helps if you get a stitch while running?
102084.e: A stitch is a stabbing pain in your side. If you slow down and breathe calmly, it usually soon goes away.
102084.m: Slowing down helps with a stitch.

102085.q: What is the big cross-country ski race in the Engadine called?
102085.e: Every March, many thousands of people take part in the Engadin Skimarathon on cross-country skis. The course goes from Maloja to S-chanf.
102085.m: The Engadin Skimarathon is a big cross-country ski race.

102086.q: How do you build up more stamina over time?
a: Through sleeping a lot during the day
102086.e: If you train often and regularly, your stamina keeps improving. The body gets used to the effort.
102086.m: You build stamina through regular training.

102087.q: What is the short form of the word metre?
102087.e: For metre you simply write a small m. For example, 5 m means five metres.
102087.m: The short form of metre is m.

102088.q: Roughly how tall is a normal door in a house?
102088.e: A door is a bit taller than a tall adult. That is about two metres.
102088.m: A door is about two metres tall.

102089.q: Which is longer: 1 metre or 90 centimetres?
102089.e: 1 metre is 100 centimetres. 100 centimetres is more than 90 centimetres.
102089.m: A metre is longer than 90 centimetres.

102090.q: How many centimetres are 2 metres and 50 centimetres together?
102090.e: 2 metres are 200 centimetres. 200 plus 50 makes 250 centimetres.
102090.m: Two metres and 50 centimetres are 250 centimetres.

102091.q: How many metres are in half a kilometre?
102091.e: A kilometre has 1000 metres. Half of that is 500 metres.

102092.q: Roughly how high is the highest mountain in Switzerland, the Dufourspitze?
102092.e: The Dufourspitze in Valais is 4634 metres high. It is the highest peak in Switzerland.
102092.m: Switzerland's highest mountain is over 4600 metres high.

102093.q: What is best measured in centimetres?
102093.e: Centimetres are good for small things. Long distances are better measured in metres or kilometres.
102093.m: Small things are measured in centimetres.

102094.q: How much are 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres together?
102094.e: You work out 3 plus 4. That makes 7 centimetres.
102094.m: You can simply add up the same units.

102095.q: Which is longer: 120 centimetres or 1 metre?
102095.e: 1 metre is 100 centimetres. So 120 centimetres is 20 centimetres more.
102095.m: 120 centimetres is more than a metre.

102096.e: A tape measure is a long, soft strip with a scale on it. You can use it to measure lengths.
102096.m: A tape measure is a bendy strip for measuring.

102097.q: What is best for measuring how big a head is all the way round?
102097.e: You can wrap a tape measure round your head. A stiff ruler won't go round round things.
102097.m: Round things are measured with a tape measure.

102098.q: Why can you measure round a tree trunk with a tape measure?
102098.e: The tape measure is soft and bends round the trunk. That is how you measure the distance round it.

102099.q: What happens with a retractable tape measure when you press the button?
102099.e: Inside the tape measure there is a spring. It pulls the metal tape back into the case.
102099.m: A retractable tape measure rolls the tape back up by itself.

102100.q: How long is a typical sewing tape measure?
102100.e: A sewing tape measure is usually 150 centimetres long. That is enough to measure a person.
102100.m: A sewing tape measure is usually 150 centimetres long.

102101.q: On sports day, what do you use to measure the distance in the long jump?
102101.e: A long tape measure reaches from the take-off to the mark in the sand. That shows exactly how far someone jumped.
102101.m: Long jumps are measured with a long tape measure.

102102.q: What can you see on a tape measure?
102102.e: On the tape measure there are lines for centimetres and millimetres. The numbers show the centimetres.
102102.m: A tape measure has numbers and lines on it.

102103.q: What does the children's doctor often use to measure how tall you are?
a: A measuring scale on the wall
102103.e: A long scale hangs on the wall, a bit like a tape measure. You stand with your back against it and your height is read off.
102103.m: Your height is measured on a measuring scale on the wall.

102104.q: What do you use to draw straight lines in your exercise book?
102104.e: A ruler has a straight edge. You run your pencil along it.
102104.m: You draw straight lines with a ruler.

102105.q: Where do you line up the ruler when you measure?
102105.e: Measuring always starts at zero. Otherwise the result is wrong.
102105.m: When you measure, you start at zero.

102106.q: What are the tiny lines between the centimetres on a ruler called?
102106.e: Between two centimetre lines there are ten small sections. Each one is a millimetre.
102106.m: The smallest lines on a ruler are millimetres.

102107.q: How long is a common school ruler?
102107.e: Many school rulers are 30 centimetres long. There are also shorter ones of 15 or 20 centimetres.
102107.m: A school ruler is often 30 centimetres long.

102108.q: What is the triangular ruler with a right angle called?
102108.e: With a set square you can measure and draw right angles. It is shaped like a triangle.
102108.m: A set square is a triangular ruler.

102109.q: A line on a ruler goes from 2 to 9 centimetres. How long is it?
102109.e: You work out 9 minus 2. The line is 7 centimetres long.
102109.m: You work out end minus start.

102110.q: What material are many school rulers made of?
102110.e: Many rulers are made of hard, see-through plastic. There are also rulers made of wood or metal.
102110.m: A ruler has to be hard and straight.

102111.q: Why don't you measure the classroom with a ruler?
a: Because the ruler is too short
Because the ruler is too heavy
Because the ruler is too soft
Because the ruler is too colourful
102111.e: You would have to put the short ruler down very many times. For long distances a tape measure is better.
102111.m: A ruler is too short for long distances.

102112.q: How many times does the short hand go all the way round in a whole day?
102112.e: A clock face only shows 12 hours. But a whole day has 24 hours. That is why the short hand goes round twice.
102112.m: The short hand goes round twice in a day.

102113.q: Which hand on a clock shows the hours?
102113.e: The short hand is called the hour hand. It moves slowly from number to number.
102113.m: The short hand shows the hours.

102114.q: Which hand on a clock moves the fastest?
102114.e: The second hand goes all the way round once every minute. The hour hand is the slowest.
102114.m: The second hand is the fastest hand.

102115.q: The long hand points to 12 and the short hand to 3. What time is it?
102115.e: When the long hand is on 12, it is exactly on the hour. The short hand points to 3, so it is 3 o'clock.
102115.m: When the long hand is on 12, it is exactly on the hour.

102116.q: What is the famous clock tower with moving figures in Bern called?
102116.e: The Zytglogge is an old tower in Bern's old town. Shortly before every full hour, figures move on it.
102116.m: The Zytglogge is the famous clock tower in Bern.

102117.q: What work is the Jura region of Switzerland famous for?
102117.e: In the Jura, for example in La Chaux-de-Fonds, watches have been made for a long time. Swiss watches are known all over the world.
102117.m: Many Swiss watches are made in the Jura.

102118.q: What do you call a clock that shows the time only with digits?
102118.e: A digital clock has no hands. It shows the time with digits, for example 08:15.
102118.m: A digital clock shows the time with digits.

102119.q: It is half past four. Which number is the long hand pointing to?
102119.e: At half past, half an hour has gone by. Then the long hand is at the bottom, on the 6.
102119.m: At half past, the long hand points to 6.

102120.q: You count slowly from 1 to 10. Roughly how long does that take?
102120.e: If you count slowly, you need about one second for each number. Up to 10 that is about 10 seconds.
102120.m: Counting slowly takes about one second per number.

102121.e: If you say “one thousand” slowly, it takes about one second. That way you can count seconds without a clock.
102121.m: Saying “one thousand” once takes about a second.

102122.q: Which device is used in sport to measure time to the exact second?
102122.e: You start a stopwatch at the start and stop it at the finish. It even shows tenths and hundredths of a second.
102122.m: Times in sport are measured with a stopwatch.

102123.q: Which is shorter: a second or a minute?
102123.e: A minute is made up of 60 seconds. So a second is much shorter.
102123.m: A second is shorter than a minute.

102124.q: How fast did Usain Bolt run when he set the 100 metres world record (as of 2026)?
102124.e: Usain Bolt from Jamaica ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds in 2009. It is still the world record today.
102124.m: The 100 metres world record is under ten seconds.

102125.q: How many minutes are three quarters of an hour?
102125.e: A quarter of an hour has 15 minutes. 3 times 15 makes 45 minutes.
102125.m: Three quarters of an hour are 45 minutes.

102126.q: How long should you brush your teeth?
102126.e: Dentists recommend brushing for about two to three minutes. That way all your teeth get clean.
102126.m: Brushing your teeth takes a few minutes.

102127.q: It is 10:50. What time is it 20 minutes later?
102127.e: It is 10 minutes until 11:00. Then there are 10 minutes left, so it is 11:10.
102127.m: After 60 minutes a new hour begins.

102128.q: How many minutes are one and a half hours?
102128.e: An hour has 60 minutes, half an hour has 30 minutes. 60 plus 30 makes 90 minutes.
102128.m: One and a half hours are 90 minutes.

102129.q: Roughly how much water fits into a full bath?
102129.e: About 150 litres of water fit into a normal bath. That is a great many bottles.
102129.m: A bath holds over a hundred litres.

102130.q: How many 1.5-litre bottles do you need for 3 litres of water?
102130.e: 1.5 litres plus 1.5 litres makes 3 litres. So you need 2 bottles.
102130.m: Two bottles of one and a half litres make three litres.

102131.q: How many 2-decilitre glasses can you fill with 1 litre?
102131.e: A litre has 10 decilitres. 10 divided by 2 makes 5 glasses.
102131.m: One litre fills five glasses of two decilitres.

102132.q: How much milk is in a typical carton of milk in the shop?
102132.e: Most milk cartons contain one litre. There are also smaller ones with half a litre.
102132.m: A milk carton usually contains one litre.

102133.q: What do you need a measuring jug for in the kitchen?
102133.e: With a measuring jug you measure how much milk, water or flour you need. That way the recipe turns out well.
102133.m: You measure out amounts with a measuring jug.

102134.q: What is printed on the outside of a measuring jug?
102134.e: The lines are called a scale. You read off from them how much is in the jug.
102134.m: A measuring jug has a scale.

102135.q: How do you read a measuring jug correctly?
102135.e: You look exactly level at the liquid. From above or below you would read the wrong amount.
102135.m: You read a measuring jug at eye level.

102136.q: You need 3 decilitres of milk. Up to which line do you fill the jug?
102136.e: One decilitre is 100 millilitres. So 3 decilitres are 300 millilitres.

102137.q: Where do you put the measuring jug when reading it?
102137.e: If the jug is tilted, the liquid is higher on one side. On a flat table the measurement is right.
102137.m: The jug must stand straight when you measure.

102138.q: You pour 200 millilitres and then 300 millilitres into the measuring jug. How much is in it?
102138.e: You work out 200 plus 300. That makes 500 millilitres.
102138.m: You can simply add millilitres to millilitres.

102139.q: Why is a measuring jug usually see-through?
a: So you can see how full it is
102139.e: Through the clear side you can see how high the liquid comes. Then you can read it off the scale.
102139.m: With a measuring jug you need to see how full it is.

102140.q: How many times do you have to fill a half-litre measuring jug to get 2 litres?
102140.e: Two half litres make one litre. So for 2 litres you need 4 half litres.
102140.m: Four half litres are two litres.

a: Sand trickles through a narrow gap
102141.e: An hourglass has two glass bulbs. The sand slowly trickles through the narrow gap from top to bottom.
102141.m: In an hourglass, sand trickles downwards.

102142.q: What do you do when all the sand is at the bottom and you want to time again?
102142.e: When you turn the hourglass over, the sand is at the top again. Then the time starts from the beginning.
102142.m: To start again, you turn the hourglass over.

102143.q: What is a small hourglass often used for in the kitchen?
102143.e: A small hourglass might run for three minutes, for example. That is why it is also called an egg timer.
102143.m: A small hourglass helps when boiling eggs.

102144.q: What are the two bulbs of an hourglass usually made of?
102144.e: The bulbs are made of glass so you can see the sand. A frame holds them together.
102144.m: An hourglass is usually made of glass.

102145.q: What is a small hourglass often used for in board games?
a: To limit the time for a turn
102145.e: When the sand is at the bottom, the time for the task is up. That way everyone has the same amount of time.
102145.m: In games, an hourglass limits the time.

102146.q: Why doesn't an hourglass need a battery?
102146.e: The Earth pulls everything downwards. This gravity makes the sand trickle.

102147.q: What happens if you lay a running hourglass flat on its side?
102147.e: When the hourglass lies flat, the sand no longer falls through the narrow gap. The timing stops.

102148.q: How long is a typical folding ruler when it is fully opened out?
102148.e: In Switzerland it is called a “metre stick”, but the usual folding ruler is two metres long. It is made of many short sections.
102148.m: A folding ruler is usually two metres long.

102149.q: Who often needs a folding ruler at work?
102149.e: Carpenters and other tradespeople measure boards and walls. A folding ruler is handy for that.
102149.m: Tradespeople often measure with a folding ruler.

102150.q: How do you make a folding ruler small enough to fit in your pocket?
102150.e: The sections of a folding ruler are joined by hinges. That way you can fold it up.
102150.m: You fold up a folding ruler.

102151.q: What material are classic folding rulers made of?
102151.e: Classic folding rulers are made of wood. But there are also plastic or metal ones.
102151.m: A classic folding ruler is made of wood.

102152.q: A folding ruler has 10 sections, each 20 centimetres long. How long is it?
102152.e: You work out 10 times 20 centimetres. That makes 200 centimetres.
102152.m: For pieces of equal length you multiply.

102153.q: What is a folding ruler better for than a ruler?
a: Drawing lines in your exercise book
102153.e: A table is longer than a ruler. With a folding ruler you can measure it in one go.
102153.m: For longer objects you use a folding ruler.

102154.q: How do you measure a 5-metre-long room with a 2-metre folding ruler?
a: I put it down several times one after another
I use a pair of scales
102154.e: You put the folding ruler down, make a mark and put it down again from there. At the end you add it all up.
102154.m: Long distances are measured in several pieces.

a: The length of one step when walking
102156.e: Stride length is the distance you cover with one step. It is a little different for every person.
102156.m: Stride length is the length of one step.

102157.q: How can you roughly measure a distance without a tape measure?
102157.e: If you know your stride length, you can pace out distances. You count your steps and do the maths.
102157.m: You can measure roughly with steps.

102158.q: Who usually takes the longer steps?
a: Everyone takes steps of the same length
102158.e: Adults have longer legs than children. That is why their steps are longer.
102158.m: Adults take longer steps than children.

102159.q: Your step is 50 centimetres long. How far do you get with 10 steps?
102159.e: 10 times 50 centimetres makes 500 centimetres. That is 5 metres.
102159.m: Stride length times number of steps gives the distance.

102160.q: Why is measuring with steps not exact?
a: The steps are not always the same length
102160.e: Sometimes you take bigger steps, sometimes smaller ones. That is why the result is only roughly right.
102160.m: Steps are never exactly the same length.

102161.e: A pedometer senses every movement as you walk. That is how it counts your steps during the day.

102162.q: Roughly how long is a normal step of an adult?
102162.e: When walking calmly, an adult's step is about 70 centimetres long. For tall people it is a bit more.
102162.m: An adult's step is a little less than a metre long.

102163.q: How do you find out your own stride length?
a: Walk 10 steps, measure and divide by 10
102163.e: You walk 10 normal steps and measure the whole distance. If you divide by 10, you know the length of one step.
102163.m: Measuring many steps makes the result more exact.

102164.q: Which old unit of length was about as long as a forearm?
102164.e: In the past people measured with parts of the body. The cubit was the length of the forearm.
102164.m: In the past, lengths were measured with parts of the body.

102165.e: Wood is the hard material in the trunk, branches and roots of trees and shrubs.

102166.q: Which tree has especially light wood that is used for model aeroplanes?
102166.e: Balsa wood is one of the lightest woods in the world. That is why people like to build model aeroplanes from it.

102167.q: What happens to dry wood when you put it in water?
102167.e: Most woods are lighter than water because they contain a lot of air. That is why they float.

102168.q: Which tree is a common conifer for building timber in Switzerland?
102168.e: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is widely used for building.
102168.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.

102169.q: What do you call wood that is still fresh and wet?
102169.e: Freshly felled wood still contains a lot of water. It is called green wood or fresh wood.
102169.m: Fresh wood still contains a lot of water.

102170.q: Who works with wood and builds roof frames from it?
102170.e: A carpenter builds roof frames, wooden houses and stairs from large wooden beams.
102170.m: A carpenter builds roof frames from wood.

a: Thin layers of wood glued crosswise
102171.e: Plywood is made of several thin layers of wood glued together crosswise. This makes it strong and it hardly warps.
102171.m: Plywood is made of glued layers of wood.

102172.q: Why is wood considered a renewable raw material?
a: Because it is pumped out of the ground
Because it is made in a laboratory
102172.e: If you fell trees and plant new ones, more wood grows again. That is why wood is a renewable raw material.
102172.m: Wood is a renewable raw material.

102173.e: Firewood is burnt in a stove, a fireplace or a campfire. It gives warmth and light.
102173.m: Firewood gives warmth when it burns.

102174.q: Why should firewood dry before it is burnt?
102174.e: Wet wood burns badly and makes a lot of smoke. Dry wood burns hot and clean.
102174.m: Dry wood burns better than wet wood.

102175.q: How long is fresh firewood usually left to dry?
102175.e: Freshly split firewood usually needs one to two years in the open air until it is dry enough.
102175.m: Firewood dries for one to two years.

102177.q: What is a split piece of firewood called?
102177.e: A split piece of wood for the stove is called a log.
102177.m: A piece of firewood is called a log.

102178.q: Which tool do you use to split pieces of wood?
102178.e: With an axe or a splitting maul you split pieces of wood lengthwise.
102178.m: You split wood with an axe.

102179.q: Which saw has a chain and a motor?
102179.e: A chainsaw has a moving chain with teeth that is driven by a motor. Foresters use it to fell trees.
102179.m: A chainsaw has a chain with teeth.

102180.q: Which fine saw do children use in craft lessons to cut shapes out of thin wood?
102180.e: A fretsaw has a very thin blade. You can use it to cut fine curves and shapes.
102180.m: You cut fine shapes with a fretsaw.

102182.q: Which saw has a round blade that spins quickly?
102182.e: A circular saw has a round blade that a motor spins very fast. It gets its name from the circle.
102182.m: A circular saw has a round blade.

102183.q: What protects your ears when working with a loud chainsaw?
102183.e: Chainsaws are very loud. Ear defenders protect the ears. You also wear a helmet, safety goggles and gloves.
102183.m: With loud saws, ear defenders protect your ears.

102184.q: What do you use to hold a piece of wood firmly while sawing?
102184.e: A clamp fixes the wood to the table. That way it doesn't slip while you saw.
102184.m: When sawing, the wood must be held firmly.

102185.q: Which animal gnaws down trees and builds dams from the wood?
102185.e: The beaver fells trees with its strong teeth. It builds dams and lodges from branches and trunks.
102185.m: The beaver builds dams from wood.

102186.q: Which of these woods is the hardest?
102186.e: Oak is a heavy hardwood. Spruce, balsa and poplar are softer.

102187.q: Which piece of wooden furniture has a seat and a back?
102187.e: You sit on a chair. It has a seat, legs and a backrest.

102188.q: Which piece of furniture is usually made of wood and has four legs and a top?
102188.e: A table has a tabletop and usually four legs. Many tables are made of wood.
102188.m: A table has a top and legs.

102189.q: What is the job of someone who makes furniture from wood?
102189.e: A cabinetmaker, also called a joiner, makes furniture, doors and windows from wood.
102189.m: A cabinetmaker makes furniture from wood.

102190.e: You work with wood at a workbench. It is very sturdy and often has a vice.
102190.m: A workbench is a work table for craftspeople.

102191.q: What do you use to protect wooden furniture so that it shines nicely?
102191.e: Oil, wax or varnish protects the wooden surface from dirt and moisture and gives it a nice shine.
102191.m: Oil, wax or varnish protects wooden furniture.

102192.q: Which piece of wooden furniture do you need for sleeping?
102192.e: You sleep in a bed. Many bed frames are made of wood.

102193.q: Where do you usually keep books?
102193.e: A bookcase has shelves one above the other. You put books and other things on them.

102194.q: What do you use to join the wooden parts of a piece of furniture firmly?
102194.e: Furniture parts are joined firmly with screws, nails, wooden dowels and glue.
102194.m: Screws and glue hold furniture together.

102195.q: Which piece of furniture has drawers?
102195.e: A chest of drawers is a low cupboard with several drawers for clothes and other things.
102195.m: A chest of drawers has drawers.

102196.q: Which bird pecks holes in tree trunks with its beak?
102196.e: The woodpecker hammers holes into wood with its hard beak. That is how it finds beetle larvae and makes its nesting hole.
102196.m: The woodpecker pecks holes in tree trunks.

102197.q: What does a tree trunk carry upwards from the roots?
102197.e: In the trunk, water with nutrient salts rises from the roots all the way up to the leaves.
102197.m: The trunk carries water up from the roots.

102198.q: Where are felled tree trunks taken to be made into planks?
102198.e: At the sawmill the trunks are sawn into planks and beams. Houses and furniture are built from them.
102198.m: At the sawmill, trunks are made into planks.

102199.q: Who fells the trees in the forest?
102199.e: In Switzerland, foresters fell the trees and look after the forest. Cabinetmakers and carpenters work with the wood later.
102199.m: The forester fells trees in the forest.

102200.q: What is the part of a tree that stays in the ground after felling called?
102200.e: After felling, a short piece with the roots stays in the ground. It is called a tree stump.
102200.m: After felling, the tree stump is left standing.

102201.q: How does a tree trunk change every year?
a: It always stays the same thickness
102201.e: Under the bark, a new layer of wood grows every year. So the trunk gets a little bit thicker every year.
102201.m: A tree trunk gets thicker every year.

102202.q: What do you call a boat made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk?
102202.e: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk. The lake dwellers of the Stone Age already used them to cross the lakes.
102202.m: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a tree trunk.

102203.q: What is right in the middle of a tree trunk?
102203.e: Right in the middle of the trunk is the pith. The layers of wood grow around it, and the bark is on the outside.
102203.m: The pith is in the middle of the trunk.

102204.q: Why does a tree have bark?
102204.e: Bark protects the tree like a skin against cold, heat, fungi and animals.
102204.m: Bark protects the tree like a skin.

102205.q: Which tree has white bark with black patches?
102205.e: You can easily recognise the birch by its white bark with dark patches.

102206.q: Which tree has smooth, grey bark?
102206.e: The beech keeps smooth, silvery grey bark even when it is old. Most other trees get cracked bark.
102206.m: The beech has smooth, grey bark.

102207.q: Which spice is actually dried tree bark?
102207.e: Cinnamon comes from the bark of the cinnamon tree. The bark rolls up into sticks as it dries.

102208.q: Which bird taps on bark to find insects underneath?
102208.e: The woodpecker hammers on the bark with its strong beak. It pulls insects out with its long tongue.
102208.m: The woodpecker looks for insects under the bark.

102209.q: What do you call the outer, often cracked layer of a tree trunk?
102209.e: The outer dead layer of the trunk is the bark. On old trees it is often thick and cracked.
102209.m: The outer layer of the trunk is the bark.

102210.q: What happens to the bark when a tree gets thicker?
102210.e: Because the trunk grows, the old bark becomes too tight and cracks. That is why old trunks are often cracked.
102210.m: When the trunk grows, the bark cracks.

102211.q: What is shredded bark used for in the garden?
102211.e: Bark mulch covers the soil in flower beds. It keeps the earth moist and holds back weeds.
102211.m: Bark mulch keeps the soil in the bed moist.

102212.q: What does a growth ring in a tree trunk show?
102212.e: Every year a new layer of wood grows. In a cross-section you see it as a ring.
102212.m: A growth ring shows one year of growth.

102213.q: A tree stump has 25 growth rings. About how old was the tree?
102213.e: Each growth ring stands for one year. So 25 rings mean about 25 years.
102213.m: You count the growth rings to estimate a tree's age.

102214.q: Where on a tree can you count the growth rings easily?
a: On a cross-section of the trunk
102214.e: If you saw straight across a trunk, you can see the growth rings on the cut surface.
102214.m: You see growth rings on a sawn trunk.

102215.q: What does a wide growth ring mean?
a: The tree grew well that year
102215.e: In a good year with enough water and warmth, the tree grows a lot. Then the growth ring is wide.
102215.m: A wide growth ring shows a good year for growth.

102216.q: Where is the youngest growth ring?
a: Right on the outside, under the bark
102216.e: The new layer of wood always grows on the outside, just under the bark. The oldest ring is on the inside.
102216.m: The youngest growth ring is right on the outside.

102217.q: Why can you see growth rings at all?
a: Wood from spring and summer looks different
102217.e: In spring, light, loose wood grows, and in late summer darker, firmer wood. This makes a visible ring every year.
102217.m: Light and dark wood together form one growth ring.

102218.q: What do very narrow growth rings usually mean?
a: A difficult year, for example a drought
102218.e: In drought or cold, the tree grows little. Then the growth ring is narrow.
102218.m: Narrow growth rings show a difficult year.

102219.q: What do people do in a sawmill?
102219.e: In a sawmill, tree trunks are sawn into planks, beams and battens.
102219.m: In a sawmill, trunks are sawn into planks.

102220.q: What used to drive the saw in an old sawmill by a stream?
102220.e: Sawmills used to stand by streams. The water turned a water wheel, and the water wheel drove the saw.
102220.m: Old sawmills were driven by water power.

102221.q: What is a long, thick, square piece of wood for building houses called?
102221.e: A beam is a thick, square-edged piece of wood. It is used to build roof frames, for example.
102221.m: A beam is a thick piece of wood for building.

102222.q: What do you call a flat, thin piece of sawn wood?
102222.e: A plank is flat and much wider than it is thick. Planks are made from the trunk in the sawmill.
102222.m: A plank is a flat piece of wood.

102223.q: How are fresh planks dried after sawing?
a: Stacked with air between the planks
102223.e: The planks are stacked with small strips of wood in between. That way air can flow through and the wood can dry.
102223.m: Planks dry in stacks in the open air.

102224.q: What is made from the wood leftovers of a sawmill?
102224.e: Sawdust, shavings and leftovers are used again, for example for pellets, chipboard or as firewood.
102224.m: Wood leftovers from the sawmill are used again.

102225.q: What does a lorry bring to the sawmill?
102225.e: Lorries carry the felled tree trunks from the forest to the sawmill.
102225.m: Lorries bring tree trunks to the sawmill.

102226.q: What does a machine in the sawmill remove from the tree trunk first?
102226.e: Before a trunk is sawn, a machine peels off the bark. This step is called debarking.
102226.m: Before sawing, the trunk is debarked.

102227.q: What do you call paper made from waste paper?
102227.e: Recycled paper is made from collected waste paper. This protects forests and saves energy.
102227.m: Recycled paper is made from waste paper.

102228.e: Like paper, cardboard is made of fibres, but it is thicker and stronger. Boxes are made from it.

102229.q: What is paper usually made from?
102229.e: Wood fibres and water make a pulp. This is put on a screen, pressed and dried. That is how paper is made.
102229.m: Paper is usually made from wood.

102230.q: What do people in Switzerland often do with waste paper?
a: Bundle it up and take it to the collection
102230.e: In many Swiss municipalities, waste paper is bundled up and picked up on collection days, often by school classes too.
102230.m: Waste paper is bundled up and collected.

102231.q: Which paper is especially soft and meant for your nose?
102231.e: Paper tissues are made of soft, thin layers of paper. They are meant for your nose.

102232.q: In which Swiss city is there an old paper mill where paper is still made by hand?
102232.e: The Basel Paper Mill is a museum in an old mill on the Rhine. Paper is still made by hand there.
102232.m: At the Basel Paper Mill, paper is made by hand.

a: The bark of the cork oak
102233.e: Cork is the thick, light bark of the cork oak. This oak grows in warm countries around the Mediterranean.
102233.m: Cork is the bark of the cork oak.

102234.q: What is cork often used for?
102234.e: Cork is tight and springy. That is why it is used to close bottles.
102234.m: Corks are used to close bottles.

102235.q: What does cork do in water?
a: It goes as hard as stone
102235.e: Cork is very light and full of air. That is why it floats well on water.

102236.q: Which country has the most cork oaks?
102236.e: Portugal is the most important country for cork oaks and cork. The trees need a warm, dry climate.
102236.m: Portugal has the most cork oaks.

102237.q: How often can you strip the bark off a cork oak?
102237.e: After stripping, the cork bark grows back. Only after about nine years is it thick enough again.
102237.m: A cork oak is stripped about every nine years.

102238.q: Which piece of school equipment is often made of cork?
102238.e: You can pin notes to a cork pinboard with drawing pins. The cork holds the pins firmly.
102238.m: Drawing pins hold well in a cork pinboard.

102239.q: Do you have to fell a cork oak to get cork?
a: No, you only strip the bark
Yes, and you dig it up
102239.e: The cork oak stays standing and lives on. Only the outer bark is carefully stripped off.
102239.m: You don't have to fell the cork oak for cork.

102240.e: Cork is made of tiny air-filled cells. That is why it is light and gives a little.
102240.m: Cork is light and a bit soft.

a: A sticky liquid from a tree
102241.e: Resin is a sticky substance made mainly by conifers. It oozes out when the bark is damaged.
102241.m: Resin is a sticky liquid from a tree.

102242.q: Why does a tree make resin?
102242.e: If the bark is damaged, resin flows into the wound. It seals it and keeps fungi and insects away.
102242.m: Resin seals wounds on a tree.

102243.q: What do you call fossilised, very old resin?
102243.e: Amber is tree resin that hardened in the ground millions of years ago. It is often golden yellow.
102243.m: Amber is very old, hardened resin.

102244.q: Which trees have especially a lot of resin?
a: Conifers such as spruces and pines
102244.e: Above all, conifers such as spruce, pine and larch make a lot of resin.
102244.m: Conifers have especially a lot of resin.

102245.q: What does resin often smell like?
102245.e: Resin has a spicy, fresh scent. You know this smell from conifer forests.
102245.m: Resin smells spicy, like the forest.

102246.q: What do violinists rub with resin?
a: The hairs of the violin bow
102246.e: Violin resin is called rosin. It makes the bow hairs grip, so that the strings sound.
102246.m: Resin makes the violin bow grip.

102247.q: What is resin like when it comes fresh out of the tree?
102247.e: Fresh resin is thick and very sticky. Only over time does it become solid.

102248.q: What can you sometimes find inside amber?
102248.e: Long ago, insects got stuck in the sticky resin. When the resin hardened, they were preserved inside it.
102248.m: You sometimes find insects in amber.

102249.q: What is a typical Swiss chalet built from?
102249.e: A chalet is a wooden house of the kind known in the Alps. It often stands on a stone base.
102249.m: A chalet is a wooden house from the mountains.

102250.q: What shape is the roof of a typical chalet?
102250.e: Chalets usually have a gently sloping gable roof that sticks out far beyond the walls. It protects against rain and snow.
102250.m: The chalet roof sticks out far beyond the walls.

102251.q: What does a chalet often have in front of the windows?
102251.e: Typical features are wooden shutters and window boxes with geraniums on the balcony.
102251.m: Chalets often have shutters and flowers.

102252.q: Where in Switzerland are there especially many chalets?
102252.e: Chalets are found mainly in the Alps and the Pre-Alps, for example in the Bernese Oberland or Valais.
102252.m: Chalets are found mainly in the mountains.

102253.q: Which language does the word “chalet” come from?
102253.e: The word “chalet” comes from the French of western Switzerland. It originally meant an alpine hut.

102254.q: Why does the wood of old chalets turn dark brown on the sunny side?
102254.e: Sunlight changes the wood over the years. That is why old wood turns dark brown on the sunny side.
102254.m: The sun darkens the wood of old chalets.

102255.q: What is often written on old wooden houses in the Bernese Oberland?
a: A saying or the year it was built
102255.e: On many old wooden houses, sayings, names and the year of building are carved or painted into the beams.
102255.m: Old wooden houses often carry sayings and the year they were built.

102256.q: What is a simple hut on an alpine pasture, where herders live in summer, called?
102256.e: On the alpine pasture, herders live in an alpine hut in summer. They often make cheese there too.
102256.m: Herders live in the alpine hut in summer.

102351.q: In which unit is a child's height usually given?
102351.e: Height is a length. Lengths are measured in centimetres or metres.

102352.q: At what time of day is a person a tiny bit taller?
102352.e: Lying down at night lets the spine recover. That is why you are about 1 to 2 centimetres taller in the morning than in the evening.
102352.m: You are a little taller in the morning than in the evening.

102353.q: Up to what age do most people grow taller?
102353.e: Most people stop growing taller somewhere between about 16 and 20. After that, their height stays the same for a long time.
102353.m: At about 18 to 20, you have finished growing.

102354.q: Who does a child's height depend on to a large extent?
102354.e: Height is inherited from the parents to a large extent. Tall parents often have tall children.
102354.m: You inherit your height partly from your parents.

102355.q: Lina is 120 cm tall and Tim is 130 cm tall. How many centimetres taller is Tim?
102355.e: You work out 130 minus 120 = 10. So Tim is 10 centimetres taller.
102355.m: You find the difference by subtracting the smaller number.

102356.q: Mia was 115 cm tall. A year later she is 121 cm tall. How much has she grown?
102356.e: You work out 121 minus 115 = 6. Mia has grown 6 centimetres in a year.
102356.m: You work out growth as new height minus old height.

102357.q: What helps a child grow healthily?
102357.e: The body needs building blocks from healthy food to make bones and muscles. Sleep and exercise also help.

102358.q: What do you need a height chart on the wall for?
102358.e: Centimetres are printed on a height chart. You stand in front of it and see how tall you are.
102358.m: You measure your height with a height chart.

102359.q: What is the right way to stand at a height chart?
102359.e: Shoes would make you taller and bent knees shorter. That is why you stand barefoot and straight.
102359.m: At the height chart, you stand barefoot and straight.

102360.q: What do you lay flat on your head when measuring at a height chart?
a: A book or a small board
102360.e: A flat book or board shows exactly where your head ends. That way you can read the number on the wall easily.
102360.m: A flat book on your head helps you read the height.

102361.q: Why do people often write the date next to the line on a height chart?
a: To see when you were that tall
Because otherwise you forget the name
102361.e: With the date, you can compare later. That way you see how much you have grown over a period of time.
102361.m: The date shows when you were how tall.

102362.q: A line on the height chart is at 100 cm. How many metres is that?
102362.e: 100 centimetres is exactly 1 metre. So anyone standing there is 1 metre tall.
102362.m: A line at 100 centimetres means 1 metre.

102363.q: Leo's line was at 110 cm last year. Today it is at 117 cm. How much has Leo grown?
102363.e: You work out 117 minus 110 = 7. Leo has grown 7 centimetres.
102363.m: The gap between two lines shows the growth.

102364.q: How many millimetres are there in one centimetre on the height chart?
102364.e: There are 10 small lines between two centimetre lines. Each of them is a millimetre.

102365.q: How must a height chart hang so that it measures correctly?
a: With the zero at the floor
With the zero at the ceiling
At an angle on the wall
In the middle of the door
102365.e: Height is measured from the floor you are standing on. That is why the start of the height chart must be exactly at the floor.
102365.m: The height chart starts at the floor.

102366.q: What are a child's first teeth called?
102366.e: The first teeth are called milk teeth. They fall out later and are replaced.
102366.m: The first teeth are called milk teeth.

102367.q: Why should you brush milk teeth well, even though they fall out later?
a: They keep space for the new teeth
Otherwise they turn into gold teeth
102367.e: Milk teeth keep the space free for the permanent teeth. Unhealthy milk teeth can also harm the new teeth.
102367.m: Healthy milk teeth are important for the new teeth.

102368.q: What do you call the set of teeth a child has while they have both milk teeth and permanent teeth?
102368.e: While the teeth are changing, old and new teeth are in the mouth together. This set of teeth is called mixed dentition.
102368.m: While your teeth are changing, you have mixed dentition.

102369.q: At about what age does most children's first milk tooth fall out?
102369.e: The change of teeth usually starts at about 6. For some children a little earlier, for others a little later.
102369.m: At about 6, your teeth start to change.

102370.q: What do you call a loose milk tooth just before it falls out?
102370.e: When the new tooth pushes from below, the milk tooth becomes loose and wobbles. It is called a wobbly tooth.
102370.m: A loose milk tooth is called a wobbly tooth.

102371.q: What pushes a milk tooth out when your teeth change?
102371.e: The permanent tooth grows under the milk tooth. It pushes upwards until the milk tooth becomes loose.
102371.m: The new tooth pushes the milk tooth out.

102372.q: What do you call the new teeth that come after the milk teeth?
102372.e: The new teeth are called permanent teeth. They only grow once and have to last a lifetime.
102372.m: After the milk teeth come the permanent teeth.

102373.q: Which made-up character collects the milk tooth that has fallen out in many stories?
102373.e: In many families, the milk tooth is put under the pillow. The tooth fairy brings a little surprise in return.
102373.m: The tooth fairy collects milk teeth.

102374.q: Which teeth appear right at the back at about age 6 without a milk tooth falling out?
102374.e: At about 6, the first permanent molars grow behind the milk teeth. That is why they are also called six-year molars.
102374.m: At about 6, the first big molars come through at the back.

102375.e: Shoe size depends on the length of your foot. The longer your foot, the bigger the number.
102375.m: Shoe size depends on the length of your foot.

102376.q: Why do children often need new shoes?
102376.e: Children's feet grow quickly. That is why their shoes soon get too small and they need bigger ones.
102376.m: Because your feet grow, you need new shoes.

102377.q: How much space should there be at the front of a shoe in front of your toes?
102377.e: When you walk, your foot slides forward a little in the shoe. That is why you need about a thumb's width of space at the front.
102377.m: There should be about a thumb's width of space at the front of the shoe.

102378.q: Which shoe size is most likely to fit a kindergarten child?
102378.e: Children of kindergarten age often wear shoe sizes around 26 to 30 (European sizes). Sizes over 40 are mostly worn by adults.
102378.m: Small children have small shoe sizes.

102379.q: How can you tell that a shoe is too small?
102379.e: If your toes touch the front, your foot has too little room. Then the shoe pinches and can hurt.
102379.m: If your toes touch the front, the shoe is too small.

102380.q: Lars wears shoe size 30. His foot has grown. Which size comes next?
102380.e: Shoe sizes go up in steps of one. After 30 comes 31.

102381.q: At what time of day is it best to try on new shoes?
a: In the middle of the night
102381.e: During the day, your feet swell a little from standing and walking. Shoes that fit in the afternoon will not pinch later.
102381.m: It is best to try on shoes in the afternoon.

102382.q: Are your left and right feet always exactly the same length?
a: No, one is often a bit longer
No, the left one is twice as long
102382.e: In many people, one foot is a tiny bit longer. You buy shoes to fit the longer foot.
102382.m: One foot is often a little longer than the other.

102383.q: Roughly how long is a newborn baby?
102383.e: Most babies are about 48 to 54 centimetres long at birth. That is roughly half a metre.
102383.m: A newborn baby is about 50 centimetres long.

102384.q: Roughly how much does a newborn baby weigh?
102384.e: Most babies weigh between about 3 and 4 kilograms at birth. That is as heavy as a few cartons of milk.
102384.m: A newborn baby weighs about 3.5 kilograms.

102385.q: What does a newborn baby drink?
102385.e: A newborn baby gets breast milk or formula milk from a bottle. It contains everything the baby needs to grow.

102386.q: How does a baby usually show that it is hungry?
102386.e: A baby cannot talk yet. It cries to show that it needs something.
102386.m: A baby cries when it is hungry.

102387.q: At about how many months do many babies get their first tooth?
102387.e: The first milk tooth usually comes at about six months. In some babies earlier, in others later.
102387.m: The first tooth often comes at about 6 months.

102388.q: What does a baby wear because it cannot use the toilet yet?
102388.e: A baby cannot control its bladder yet. The nappy soaks everything up.

102389.q: What else is a baby in its first year called?
102389.e: A baby in its first year is called an infant. It feeds at the breast or from a bottle.
102389.m: A baby in its first year is called an infant.

102390.q: Does a baby have fewer or more bones at birth than an adult?
102390.e: A baby has around 300 bones and parts of bones. Many of them later grow together.
102390.m: A baby has more bones than an adult.

102391.q: Roughly how old is a toddler?
102391.e: After its first birthday, a child is no longer an infant. Until about 3, it is called a toddler.
102391.m: A toddler is about 1 to 3 years old.

102392.q: At about what age do many children take their first steps?
102392.e: Most children learn to walk around their first birthday. Some a little earlier, others later.
102392.m: At about 1, many children learn to walk.

102393.q: Which word do many toddlers say as one of their first?
102393.e: Short words with repeated syllables like “Mama” or “Papa” are easy to say. That is why they are often among the first words.
102393.m: Mama is often one of the first words.

102394.q: At about what age do most children no longer need a nappy during the day?
102394.e: Most children learn to use the potty or toilet between the ages of 2 and 4.
102394.m: At about 3, many children are dry during the day.

102395.q: What is a place called where toddlers are looked after while their parents work?
102395.e: In Switzerland, a nursery is called a Kita, short for Kindertagesstätte. Small children play and eat there while their parents work.
102395.m: Small children are looked after at nursery.

102396.q: At about what age does a child have all its milk teeth?
102396.e: Milk teeth come through one by one. By about two and a half to three, they are usually all there.
102396.m: By about 3, all the milk teeth are there.

102397.e: First you are a baby, then a toddler. At about 6, you become a schoolchild.
102397.m: After the baby comes the toddler, and then the schoolchild.

102398.q: Why must you keep an especially close eye on toddlers?
a: They do not know about many dangers yet
102398.e: Toddlers are curious and do not yet know what is hot, sharp or dangerous. That is why they need protecting.
102398.m: Toddlers do not know about many dangers yet.

102399.q: At what age do you legally become an adult in Switzerland?
102399.e: In Switzerland, you become an adult at 18. Then you can decide many things for yourself.
102399.m: In Switzerland, you become an adult at 18.

102400.q: From what age can you vote in federal votes in Switzerland?
102400.e: Anyone who has Swiss citizenship and is 18 years old may take part in federal votes.
102400.m: At 18, you can vote in Switzerland.

102401.q: What hair grows on the face of many adult men?
102401.e: In many men, hair grows on the chin and cheeks from their teenage years. This hair is called a beard.
102401.m: Many adult men have a beard.

102402.q: Roughly how tall is an adult man in Switzerland on average?
102402.e: Men in Switzerland are on average about 1.78 metres tall. Of course, some are taller and some shorter.
102402.m: A Swiss man is on average about 1.78 metres tall.

102403.q: From what age can you get a learner's permit for a car in Switzerland?
102403.e: Since 2021, you can get a learner's permit for a car in Switzerland at 17. You can take the test at 18 at the earliest.
102403.m: In Switzerland, you can learn to drive from 17.

102404.q: Roughly how many hours of sleep do adults need per night?
102404.e: Adults usually need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Children need more.
102404.m: Adults need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep.

102405.q: What do you call someone who is between a child and an adult?
102405.e: Between about 12 and 18, you are a young person. After that, you are an adult.
102405.m: Before becoming an adult, you are a young person.

102406.q: Who needs more sleep per night: a schoolchild or an adult?
102406.e: Children grow and learn a great deal. That is why they need more sleep than adults.
102406.m: Children need more sleep than adults.

102407.q: What else are older people called?
102407.e: Older people are called senior citizens. The word “senior” comes from Latin and means “the older one”.
102407.m: Older people are called senior citizens.

102408.q: What is the pension that older people in Switzerland get from the state called?
102408.e: AHV stands for the Swiss old-age and survivors' insurance. It pays older people in Switzerland a pension every month.
102408.m: In Switzerland, older people get an AHV pension.

102409.q: At what age do men in Switzerland normally retire (as of 2025)?
102409.e: The retirement age in Switzerland is 65 for men. For women, it is also rising to 65 by 2028.
102409.m: In Switzerland, the retirement age is 65.

102410.q: Why do many old people get a little shorter again?
a: The spine sinks down a little
102410.e: In old age, the cushions between the vertebrae get flatter. That is why you get a few centimetres shorter.
102410.m: In old age, people often get a little shorter.

102411.q: What colour does hair often turn in old age?
102411.e: In old age, hair makes less pigment. That is why it turns grey or white.
102411.m: In old age, hair often turns grey.

102412.q: What helps many older people to read small letters?
102412.e: In old age, many people see less well close up. Reading glasses make the writing sharp again.

102413.q: What appears on the skin in old age?
102413.e: With age, skin becomes thinner and less stretchy. That is why wrinkles form.
102413.m: In old age, the skin gets wrinkles.

102414.q: Roughly how old do people in Switzerland live to on average (as of 2024)?
102414.e: Women in Switzerland live to over 85 on average, men to over 82. That is among the highest in the world.
102414.m: In Switzerland, people live to over 80 on average.

102415.q: Which walking aid with wheels and handles helps many older people to walk?
102415.e: A rollator has wheels, handles and brakes. You lean on it and walk more safely.
102415.m: A rollator helps you walk safely.

102416.q: Where do children usually feel growing pains?
102416.e: Growing pains usually occur in the legs, for example in the calves, thighs or the backs of the knees.
102416.m: Growing pains are usually felt in the legs.

102417.q: When do growing pains usually happen?
a: In the evening or at night
102417.e: It is typical for the pain to come in the evening or at night. Sometimes a child wakes up because of it.
102417.m: Growing pains usually come in the evening or at night.

102418.e: Growing pains occur in children. They are not known in babies or older people.

102419.q: What often helps against growing pains?
102419.e: Gentle massage and warmth, for example a warm cushion, soothe the legs. Often a bit of comfort helps too.
102419.m: Gentle massage often helps with growing pains.

a: Yes, you have to go to hospital
Yes, you may never run again
102420.e: Growing pains are unpleasant but usually harmless. They stop by themselves.

102421.q: At what age do children often have growing pains?
102421.e: Growing pains occur mainly in children between about 3 and 12.
102421.m: Growing pains often occur between 3 and 12.

102422.q: When should you go to the doctor with leg pain?
a: If there is swelling or a fever
102422.e: If the leg is swollen or red, or the child has a fever, it is probably not growing pains. Then a doctor should take a look.
102422.m: With swelling or a fever, you go to the doctor.

102423.q: Do we know for certain that growing pains come from growing?
a: No, the cause is not completely clear
102423.e: Despite their name, it has not been proven that they come from growing. Perhaps the muscles are tired from playing during the day.
102423.m: The cause of growing pains is not completely clear.

102424.q: In which unit is body weight given?
102424.e: Weight is measured in kilograms, kg for short. Metres are for lengths, litres for liquids.
102424.m: Body weight is given in kilograms.

102425.q: Roughly how much heavier is a child at 1 year than at birth?
102425.e: A child grows very fast in its first year. At one year, it weighs about three times as much as at birth.
102425.m: At one year, a child is about three times as heavy as at birth.

102426.q: What makes up most of your body weight?
102426.e: About 60 out of every 100 parts of the human body are water. In children, it is even a little more.
102426.m: The body is mostly made of water.

102427.q: Tim weighs 30 kg and his father 80 kg. How much heavier is his father?
102427.e: You work out 80 minus 30 = 50. His father is 50 kilograms heavier.
102427.m: You find the difference in weight by subtracting.

102428.q: Roughly how much does an eight-year-old child weigh?
102428.e: Many eight-year-olds weigh roughly 22 to 30 kilograms. But every child is different.
102428.m: An eight-year-old child weighs about 25 kilograms.

102429.q: What helps you to have a healthy body weight?
102429.e: If you move a lot and eat a balanced diet, you keep your weight in the healthy range.
102429.m: Exercise and healthy food keep your weight healthy.

102430.q: Why do children get heavier over time?
a: Because their bones and muscles grow
102430.e: As you grow, your bones, muscles and organs get bigger. That is why your weight goes up too.
102430.m: When you grow, you also get heavier.

102431.q: What do you use to measure body weight?
102431.e: Bathroom scales show how many kilograms you weigh. A thermometer measures temperature.

102432.q: Nina weighs 25 kg. Her school bag weighs 3 kg. What do the scales show when she stands on them with her school bag?
102432.e: You work out 25 + 3 = 28. The scales add Nina's weight and the school bag's weight together.
102432.m: Scales add up everything that is on them.

102433.q: What do bathroom scales show when nobody is standing on them?
102433.e: Without any weight, nothing presses on the scales. That is why they show zero.

102434.q: Mum stands on the scales with the baby: 68 kg. Without the baby, Mum weighs 62 kg. How heavy is the baby?
102434.e: You work out 68 minus 62 = 6. So the baby weighs 6 kilograms.
102434.m: This is how you can weigh a baby with bathroom scales.

102435.q: Which scales do you need in the kitchen to weigh flour?
102435.e: Kitchen scales are used to weigh ingredients for cooking and baking, usually in grams.
102435.m: You weigh flour with kitchen scales.

102436.q: On a balance scale, one side sinks down. What does that mean?
102436.e: On a balance scale, the heavier side pulls down. If both are equally heavy, the beam stays level.
102436.m: On a balance scale, the heavier side sinks.

102437.q: When should you weigh yourself so that you can compare your weight well?
a: Always at the same time of day
Once in the morning, once in the evening
102437.e: During the day, your weight changes because of eating and drinking. If you always measure at the same time, you can compare better.
102437.m: Always weigh yourself at the same time of day.

102438.q: What is a baby weighed on at the children's doctor?
102438.e: Baby scales have a tray that you lay the baby in. They measure very precisely, even small differences.
102438.m: Babies are weighed on baby scales.

102439.q: What do you call your mother's mother?
102439.e: Your parents' parents are your grandparents. Your mother's mother is your grandmother.
102439.m: My mother's mother is my grandmother.

102440.q: What do you call your father's father?
102440.e: Your father's father is one of your grandparents. He is your grandfather.
102440.m: My father's father is my grandfather.

102441.q: How many grandparents does every person have?
102441.e: Everyone has a mother and a father, and each of them also has two parents. 2 + 2 = 4 grandparents.

102442.q: What do many children in German-speaking Switzerland call their grandmother?
102442.e: “Grosi” is a popular Swiss German word for grandmother. “Gotte”, on the other hand, means godmother.
102442.m: Grosi is a Swiss word for grandmother.

102443.q: What are you called when your grandparents talk about you?
102443.e: For grandparents, the children of their children are their grandchildren.
102443.m: To my grandparents, I am a grandchild.

102444.q: What are your grandparents' parents called?
102444.e: The parents of your grandparents are called great-grandparents. They are one generation older still.
102444.m: My grandparents' parents are my great-grandparents.

102445.q: How many great-grandparents does every person have?
102445.e: Each of your 4 grandparents has 2 parents. 4 times 2 makes 8 great-grandparents.

102446.q: Granny is 68 years old and Nora is 8 years old. How many years older is Granny?
102446.e: You work out 68 minus 8 = 60. Granny is 60 years older than Nora.
102446.m: You find the age difference by subtracting.

102447.q: What do many children in German-speaking Switzerland call their grandfather?
102447.e: “Grossvati” or “Grosspapi” are popular Swiss German words for grandfather. “Götti”, on the other hand, means godfather.
102447.m: Grossvati is a Swiss word for grandfather.

102448.q: In which Swiss city did Albert Einstein work at the patent office?
102448.e: Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902. His former flat on the Kramgasse is now a small museum.
102448.m: Einstein worked and lived in Bern.

102449.q: In which Swiss city did Albert Einstein study at the ETH?
102449.e: Einstein studied at the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich. Later he was also a professor there.
102449.m: Einstein studied at the ETH in Zurich.

102450.q: Which famous prize did Albert Einstein receive for the year 1921?
102450.e: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1921. It is one of the most important prizes for scientists.
102450.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

102451.q: Which famous formula comes from Albert Einstein?
102451.e: The formula E = mc² shows that mass and energy are connected. It is one of the best-known formulas in the world.
102451.m: Einstein wrote one of the most famous formulas in physics.

102452.q: What is Albert Einstein's famous theory called?
102452.e: Einstein developed the theory of relativity. Among other things, it explains how time, space and gravity are connected.
102452.m: Einstein developed the theory of relativity.

102453.q: Which citizenship did Albert Einstein receive in 1901?
102453.e: In 1901 Einstein became a citizen of Zurich and therefore Swiss. He kept his Swiss citizenship until his death.
102453.m: Einstein was also a Swiss citizen.

102454.q: Which country did Albert Einstein move to in 1933?
102454.e: Einstein left Europe in 1933 because the Nazis came to power in Germany. After that he lived in Princeton in the USA.
102454.m: Einstein lived in the USA from 1933.

102455.q: Which fruit is said to have given Isaac Newton the idea of gravity?
102455.e: According to a well-known story, Newton saw an apple fall from a tree. He wondered why it falls downwards.
102455.m: A falling apple gave Newton an idea.

102456.q: Which force did Isaac Newton explain?
102456.e: Newton explained that all objects pull on each other. This force is called gravity or gravitation.

102457.q: What was Isaac Newton at the University of Cambridge?
102457.e: Newton became professor of mathematics at Cambridge in 1669. He made many of his discoveries there.
102457.m: Newton was a professor at Cambridge.

102458.q: According to Newton, what happens to a ball at rest if nothing pushes it?
102458.e: According to Newton, an object stays at rest as long as no force acts on it. This property is called inertia.
102458.m: Without a force, a ball at rest stays where it is.

102459.q: A blown-up balloon lets air out at the back. Which way does it fly, according to Newton?
102459.e: The air is pushed backwards, and the balloon is pushed forwards just as hard. That is Newton's law of action and reaction.
102459.m: Every force has an opposite force.

102460.q: According to Newton, which body in the sky stays in its orbit because the Earth pulls on it?
102460.e: Newton realised that the same force makes the apple fall and keeps the Moon circling the Earth.
102460.m: The Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in its orbit.

102461.q: What was made at the place Isaac Newton later ran in London?
102461.e: Newton became head of the Royal Mint in London. That is where English money was made.
102461.m: Newton ran the Royal Mint in London.

102462.q: According to Newton, why does an apple fall to the ground?
102462.e: According to Newton, the Earth pulls all things towards it. That is why the apple falls down and not up.
102462.m: The Earth pulls all things towards it.

102463.q: Which title did Isaac Newton receive from the Queen in 1705?
102463.e: Queen Anne knighted Newton in 1705. Since then he has been called Sir Isaac Newton.

102464.q: How many Nobel Prizes did Marie Curie receive?
102464.e: Marie Curie received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the one in Chemistry in 1911. That makes her one of very few people with two Nobel Prizes.
102464.m: Marie Curie received two Nobel Prizes.

102465.q: Which element did Marie Curie name after her home country?
102465.e: Polonium is named after Poland, the country where Marie Curie was born.

102466.q: Which strongly radioactive element did Marie Curie discover together with her husband?
102466.e: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered radium in 1898. It glows faintly in the dark.

102467.q: What was the name of the husband Marie Curie did research with?
102467.e: Pierre Curie was a physicist too. The two did research together and received the Nobel Prize together in 1903.
102467.m: Marie Curie did research with her husband Pierre.

102468.q: What did Marie Curie mainly study?
102468.e: Marie Curie studied substances that give off radiation by themselves. This field is called radioactivity.
102468.m: Marie Curie studied substances that give off radiation.

102470.q: Which instrument was Galileo Galilei one of the first to point at the sky?
102470.e: Galileo built a telescope in 1609 and used it to look at the Moon and the planets. He made many discoveries that way.
102470.m: Galileo watched the sky with a telescope.

102471.q: Around which planet did Galileo Galilei discover moons in orbit?
102471.e: In 1610 Galileo saw small points of light circling Jupiter. They were moons of Jupiter.

102472.q: How many moons of Jupiter did Galileo Galilei discover?
102472.e: Galileo discovered four large moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Today they are called the Galilean moons.
102472.m: Galileo discovered four moons of Jupiter.

102473.q: What did Galileo Galilei claim about the Earth?
102473.e: Galileo was convinced that the Earth goes round the Sun. At the time many people believed the opposite, and he got into trouble for it.
102473.m: The Earth goes round the Sun.

102474.q: In which Italian city with a leaning tower was Galileo Galilei born?
102474.e: Galileo was born in Pisa. The city is famous for its leaning tower.

102475.q: What did Galileo Galilei discover on the Moon with his telescope?
